Vatirg • PARPWELL TO MAY: WELCOME TO JUNE. . - A MAIDEN'S SONG. The merry month has passed, Yet who would have her stay? For leafy June has come, Outrivalling even May. With stately rounded grace, June walks in rich array; More girlish gait and dress . Belonged to budding May. ' •• Her face was fair, I ween; Her laugh, a sunny ray; Dewdrops like tears of joy sz' Stood in the eyes of May. Her dress of varied hues, Her bonnet primrose gay, Her skirts of royal green, Bright livery ot May! She led the children forth, Like nursemaids to their play, And caused us romp afield, Oh, blithesome month of May! • She bade us hear the lark A-carol with its lay, And list the cuckoo's note, Oh, music-loving May Ah ! merry month soon past, - Yet who would have thee stay? If nobler June has come, • Outrivallind earlier May. So let my youthful prime , Grow richer day by day, A maidenhood of June, Improving girlish May. Good Lord! to such desires Thou wilt not say me nay; '- Let grace fulfil the hopes And blossomings of May 1 —Rev. A. H. DRYSDALE, M.A.

Good at a Pinch—The crab. Why is Ireland growing rich?--Because its capital is

Dublin. A lady who advertised for a girl "to do light house- work" received a letter from an applicant who said her health demanded sea-air, and asked to know where the ighthouse was situated. Do what you are doing while you are about it, and let other things wait. Think on what you are thinking, and, until you have thought it out or 'dropped the subject, bar the mind against other topics. "What's the difference between the regular and irre- gular Greek verbs?" was asked of a schoolboy by his uncle, in order to test his knowledge. "We get more lickings trying to learn the irregular ones," was the reply. A lady was once lamenting the ill-luck which attended her affairs, when a friend, wishing to console her, bade her "look upon the bright side." "Oh," she cried, "there seems to be no bright side !" "Then polish up the dark side," was the reply. The management of a household is as much a matter of business as the management of a shop or of a count- ing-house. It requires method, accuracy, organisation, industry, economy, discipline, tact, knowledge, and capacity for adapting means to ends. Advice !Mat be desired and sought. Let every would- be adviser remember that, however excellent and a propos . his counsel may be, if given unasked, it is, with rare exceptions, thrown away. The advice given by the physician and the lawyer is not only sought, but paid for, and it is usually more faithfully followed than any , other. Whatever is worth having is certainly worth ask- ing for, and self-respect, as well as good judgment, will withhold it until then. ANGER.—No emotion is wholly wrong or base, or with- out some missiOn to fulfil; and anger is no exception. It is originally the natural and wholesome protest of our nature again t injustice of every kind. It matters not that selfishness wrests it from other service than her own, or that the absence of self-control suffers it to rage in mad violence and to become the source of untold crimes and sorrows. Its primary object is to serve, not to thwart, the cause of justice. Paul evidently had this idea when he uttered the remarkable words, "Be ye angry, and sin not; let not the sun go down upon your wrath;" and we are all ready to admit that a man desti- tute of the capacity of anger would also be destitute of some manly characteristics. flow TO POP THE Quesriols.—A young Aberdonian, bashful, but desperately in love, finding that no notice was taken of his frequent visits to the house of his sweet- heart, summoned up sufficient courage to address the fair one thus—" Jean, I wis here on Mondayrnicht." "Ay, ye were that," acknowledged she. "An' I wis here on Tuesday nicht." "So ye were." "An' I wis here on Wednesday," continued the ardent youth. "Ay ; an' ye were here on Thursday nicht." "An' I wis here last nicht, Jean." " Weel," she said, "what if ye were?" "An lam here the nicht again." "An' what shoot it, even if ye cam' every nicht?" "What shoot it, did ye say, Jean? Div ye no begin to smell a rat?" • MUSICAL THEME AND WHAT Cam BE MADE OF IT.—This is how Miss Pellingle goes to work, according to the author of "Happy Thoughts" :—Miss Pellingle com- mences "Rousseau's Dream," with variations. Beauti- ful melody, by itself first, clear and distinct. Now the air tries to break out between alternate notes, like a pri- soner behind bars. Then we have a variation;entirely bass. Happy thought—Rousseau snoring. Then a scampering up, a meeting with the right hand, a scam- pering down, and a leap off one note into space. Then both in the middle, wobbling; then down into the bass again. Happy thought—Rousseau after a heavy supper. A plaintive variation—Rousseau in pain. Light strain, mazurka time —Rousseau kicking in his sleep. Woltz. AND WoßßY.—Work is not only harmles.s, but beneficial, because it stimulates the organism to re- cuperate. Worry exhausts not only the power which nature sets apart for action, but the vital strength upon which depends the replenishing of this power; and so by living at high pressure, which means a worried I and anxious life, we both spend interest and eat up capital, with the result that nothing less than beggary stares us in the face, and all because we will haste to be rich or famous or great, or in some way prosperous. It would be well worth while to endeavour to teach people to take things easily, and remember that most of the very best things of life, whether of mind, body, or estate, are those which come only to those who can wait, and are not to be had for pushing, hurrying, or straggling THE KAFFIR BEADTIES.—The belles often cover their faces, necks, and hands with red clay, leaving margins around the eyes and mouth, which they consider adds materially to their attractions, but which really gives them a weird, frightful appearance. They sometimes mix with this clay the juice of a strongly-scented plant, which has a broad circular leaf and grows in little knolLs, and which they call satiyasi. When women pay a visit to a distaa.t kraal, before reaching their destina- tion they often sit down by a stream, and, wetting this clay, decorate themselves, the water serving as a mirror. Some few, however, possess looking-glasses, which they have procured from the traders, when they never cease admiring themselves. They generally possess beautiful figures, although, as a rule, their faces are not pretty. FRANKNESS AND RETICENCE.—Perhaps nothing is MOM needed to make social intetcourse fruitful of the best results than the natural exercise of frankness and reti- cence. The extreme of either, unbalanced by the presence of the other, is fatal to good conversation and to social well-being. On the one hand, the man who has never learned a prudent reserve, though he may have no ill intentions, does immense injury to himself and others by disclosing what ought to be hidden and scattering impressions which can never be effaced. On the other hand, he who is naturally and habitually secretive; and who instinctively suppresses his thoughts and feelings, can never come into sympathetic relations with others or exercise a vital influence in the world. Frequently, also, his silence may be as productive of injustice as the misplaced speech of the other. ENCOURAGEMENT. Few people realise the widely different effects produced by bringing into prominence the good or the bad points of a man's character. To do the former stimulates his powers, encourages him to make fresh efforts, inspires him with hope, and paves the way for the correction of faults. To do the latter depresses the nature, produces gloom, despondency, and fear, and actually weakens the very powers which are needed to battle with the wrong. Sust as the wise phy- sician, by buildinf.,, up the general system and establishing trie healthful discharge of functions, does fate:more to eradicate disease than he could by any direct efforts upon the disease itself, s the cheerful encouragement of all that is good in the character of a man will be more effectual in restraining faults than any direct attack on the faults and errors themselves. MASHING A MAsmine.—A young masher walking up and down the platform of a railway station in Scotland with a companion who had come to see him off observed two handsome girls enter a firat-class carriage. "Look hero," he said to his companion, who did not pay much attention to his dress—",l'll get into that same compart- ment, and I'll tell you what I want you to do. When the train is about to start, you come up and touch your hat, and say to me. 6 my.iord, the guns and dogs are in the van." His companion smiled assent, but said he doubted if be could do it with the proper air of a noble- man's servant. The maslifsr took his seat with a lordly air ia the same carriage with the young ladies whose nterest he wished to excite. The moment arrived, and the train began to move, when his compion came up to the carriage window. div.head: NOTES ON AGRICULTURR, HORTICULTURE, &c.
div.p: NOTES ON AGRICULTURR, HORTI- CULTURE, &c.

As another proof of agricultural depression, Lord Ailes- bury states that he is £15,000 a year out of pocket by the present depressed condition of things. The Prince of Wales has purchased two valuable stallions to remain at Sandringham for the use of his tenants and neighbours, at a nominal charge, and ex- presses his hope that "this may induce many of those who have hitherto hesitated to do so, to purchase some mares and try a little horse breeding." Richard Copland, a daryrnan and cowkeeper, living at Upper Norwood, has been fined 408. and costs for not having a proper water supply on *his premises. The defendant had had his water supply cut, and there was only a small pool of dirty water on the premises for the cattle. The defence was that the animals went else- where to drink. Cow SUCKING HEUSELF.—Can any of your readers suggest a remedy for a cow suckingherself ? Were she not a valuable* Jersey, and, when well-behaved, a first- , rate milker, no doubt fattening and the butcher would be I the best plan, for at times only a few pints are forth- coming at milking time; but if there is any effectual remedy we are unwilling to proceed to such ell:ernes. Spiked muzzles, cradles, and even the presence:llsf new- born twin calves have had no effect in overcoming the pernicious habit.—H.C.S. COWS CALVING PREMATITRELY.—That COWS calving pre- maturely is an infectious disease has been proyed over and over again. If a cow slips her calf and she be re- tained on the farm she is very liable to do it a second time, or if she be tied up in a stall next to another to whom this has already happened, she would be most likely to follow this example if she were at about the I same stage of pregnancy. If a bull serves a cow that I has just slipped her calf, he also appears to become in- fected, and the same cow may be repeatedly served by him without being in calf. SHEEP LAMENESS.—" An Old Subscriber" says :—My flock is much troubled with lameness, and I shall feel obliged by your kindly suggesting the best remedy.—l i presume it s ordinary " foot-rot" that causes the lame- ness of your sheep. To cure this there are numerous remedies advocated, but perhaps one of the most effec- tual and simple is the application, by means of a feather, of the butyr of antimony; but, Wore doing this, it is necessary to thoroughly pare away with a knife all the diseased portions of the hoof. In mild cases, one part of butyr of antimony mixed with four parts of tar may be applied with success.
THE RISE AND'FALL IN THE RICES OF SHORT-

HORN CATTLE. (FROM AN AGRICULTURAL CORRESPONDENT.) At the present time the mutations of prices irhich have occurred in the value of Shorthorns of recent years are fresh comparatively in the minds of most men who are interested in the breed, but as years go by these recollections grow fainter, and mistakes creep in, viz., prices are frequently enhanced by confused memories, and errors are thus propagated and perpetuated. To- day, especially in the Northern and Midland counties, throughout Scotland, and in a not much less degree in Ireland, the Shorthorn is the favourite cow of the tenant farmers and of dairymen. In effecting this, the leading herds have played the chief part, for it is to sires from such herds that the breed Ms been so widely disseminated and improved. Perhaps the history of no other herd offers so correct a synopsis of the rise and decline in prices as does that of the Duke of Devonshire at Holker, North Lancashire, and a record of the sales, showing the mutations in prices over a period of forty years will be valuable for future reference, and as such we give it to our readers. At a sale held prior to 1851, the average of the cattle sold was 22 guineas. In September of 1851, Mr. Straf- ford, of London, held a public sale of the then entire herd, consisting of 56 head, which realised a total of £1,407, or an average of £25 2s. 6d. 1 hree years later, in 1854, Mr. Strafford was again at Holker, and sold 30 head of cattle for a total of £1,984 10s., an average of £66 35., a substantial increase upon the preceding sale, and indicating that the breed was making satisfactory headway, for three bulls and three cows each made over 100 guineas, one of the former selling for 210 guineas. The next public sale was in 1871, at which 43 head of cattle were brought into the ring, and a very substantial rise in price was again realised, as is shown in the fol- lowing figures :

CHAPTER-111.

div.head: ON THE ROAD TO DRIENABOG.
div.p: ON THE ROAD TO DRIENABOG.
What bath life been? What will it be? How have I lived without thee? How Is life both lost and found in thee?— Lord ,Lytton.

-Hyacinth had not traversed more than a quarter of a • nine on her way to Drumabog, when she suddenly beheld a man's figure, some way ahead of her, leaning against a tree, and a second look showed her that the man was Vincent Lorraine. -Her heart..gave a quick throb of something Very like indignation She could not well avoid the impression that he was waiting for her; this was not his road to Curramore, and he might easily havefound out that it was the way to the Wood Cottage. It was impossible to avoid him, even if there „ , had been any turning off the road before that which led to Drnmabog, for he had seen her already, though he did not stir till she was much nearer, and then he quietly moved from his easy posture and came out into the road to Meet her, as coolly as if, on the strength of two previous chance mdetings, he had a right to waitli for her, and perhaps walk with her. • "Do you know," he said, "I did not deserve quite such a sweeping condemation as you dealt to me just now. Did you really think I would turn those people out to sleep on the heath while their child was sick ?" "I am sure you would not do it when the actual time came," said Hyacinth, "but you did not seem inclined to budge an inch." "Well, more than an inch. I should have served the• notice if you had not spoken, but without, in my own mind,-any intention of enforcing it at the date of ful- filment if the child was 'still ill. That was hard enough, I suppose?" "Not hard in reality, Mr. Lorraine, and I am sorry I wronged you—"- "That was my own fault, Miss Desmond;. but it is hardly politico seem even more unfeeling than I am. But I don't care to earn' good-will among fellows like Grady and Doolan. It would be no gain; they have got a fixed notion about the land, and they would shoot an archangel as readily as they would an archfiend, if he asked for the rent." "That is true, "said Hyacinth. sighing, "I know Grady will neither pay his rent, nor go out." • "I would not take the rent, Miss Desmond, if he offered it to•morrow,"s.aid Lorraine. I don't mean to come here 'every two or three. years to prove at the sword's point that lam master on my own laud. Of course—(shrugging his shoulders)--no one else would take the farm, and everything would go to wreck. The whole estate may go 0 wreck before it shall feed men who claim my place." "I feel as you do, Mr. Lorraine," said Hyacinth, her eyes flashing, "but yon' carry your life in your hand while you fight the battle." "I know that; and Grady intends to shoot Me before he goes out bf his farm. I don't know whether this billet clau.v came from him; the campaign is opening early. But lam detaining you. Will von allow me the honour of escorting you home, or"—he smiled as if perfectly aware that he would not be very welcome at the Wood Cottage—" part of the way home?" "I am going to Drumabog," returned Hyacinth, "where my cousins live." Lorraine noted the plural number, but only con- cerned himself with the singular. and thought it most probable•that Hyacinth did so too; but what was this "country cousin.'" to him? His rivalry would be rather a joke; and it did not at all occur to Mr. Vincent Lor- raine that there could be any danger in the joke. Take pity on me, Miss Desmond,"' he said, "and endure me at least to the verge of Drttmahog Park." "There is no park," said Hyacinth laughing, "and you would think the kronnds shabby enough with your English notions; but I am not ashamed of them." "Nor would I be, Miss Desmond.. I judge people— not places." "That is fortunate out here," said Hyacinth, gravely. "This is the Drumabog road, Mr. Lorraine"—and to- gether they turned into it—" for the places are not much. This world's goods have not fallen in large share to my country; and some of us try to drive away what we have. You have had a threatening letter already ?" "This is it," putting it into her hands. A not over clean scrap of paper, embellished with a death's head and cross-bones, and a rude sketch of a coffin, and beneath these words : " Misther lorane tak car yer a tied man if ye thry fer Hints we give ye toim iv ye dont talc this look out fer a Bullit threw yer scul from a molly maguir Man." Lorraine laughed as Hyacinth read, but the girl looked grave. , "I don't know who *rote it," she said, ".but it is meant, and you will never find out the writer—they'll never inform." "I shall make no attempt to discover the writer," said the young man, unconcernedly, and he tore the scrap into halt', and threw the fragments on the path. "Miss Desmond, this seems a very wild district—l mean there seem to be so few people living about. I feeP like St. Simon Stylites at Curramore ; from the central tower I can see miles round, and I don't think there are a dozen houses of gentry." - "And that is over a range of ,nearly twenty miles," said Hyacinth. "You must not come here for society, Mr. Lorraine. Still we have balls and such things now and then." "Where do the people come from?" "From other counties, some of them ; some from Galway and Roscommon., and then, they return next day. It is only Mrs. O'Conor who does anything grand —the rest of us are all too poor. Her place is Clan- morris House--it is about five miles from Cnrramore ; you can see it among the trees." "I noticed it. And she has a daughter, Dorine, and a son, Terence, who is in the Lancers. Margaret Finnigan is my informant. I suppose you know them very well ?" "Oh, yes; we all know each other about here. I have ridden on Terence's shoulder when he was a tall schoolboy and I a tiny child. He's coming back soon; we have not seen him for a year." Lorraine looked at the girl keenly, though covertly. Her frank sister-like way of speaking of Terence O'Conor was not much of a guide to her feelings, which might be warmer than she had any idea of. This wild, sweet colleen of the Connaught hills was not like a London girl of the same age, or even two years younger' ; and she had not seen Terence for a year. Mr. Vincent Lorraine had so mucrt of the finesse of a woman's mind that he had a far better insight into women's natures than most men of his, or any age; and then he had seen much ti women, good, bad, and indifferent —more than enough of the two latter classes—so that Hyacinth was not quite an enigma to him, though her pure, noble, earnest nature, her manner half childlike, half womanly, so utterly free from self-consciousness. or coquetry, despite her exquisite beauty, came to him as a revelation. She seemed an embodiment of all fair images of purity and freshness—the golden dawn— the mountain spring—the summer flowers—and only to look on her was to feel the whole earth changed, and all pleasure emptiness on which she could smile. herefore, he would have liked very much to discover what Hyacinth thought of this Terence O'Conor, Vitt could hardly find out what—if it had any existence— Hyacinth herself had not discovered. He tried the cousin next. "Is your cousin, then, Mr. Mansfield, in the army?" he asked, knowing he was not. Hyacinth shook her head. "No; he looks after his land." "A dull life, I should think." "Don't you ever live in the country, Mr. Lorraine?' " Som-times—in the autumn. I couldn't live there, )ou know, and look after things myself—it would be a bore, besides, I don't understand them." "Don't you ?" il acinth opened her great soft eyes wide. "Don't you know now, what the crop is in this field?"

Lorraine looked at the crop for the first time. "No," h said, " what is it ? " "Bean," said Hyacinth, laughing, "and the next field has turnips, and the next swedes.' "My sight is very long, but I cannot see any differ- ence, Miss Desmond, between the swedes and the turnips." "I can," answered Hyacinth. "I can't help knowing all those things—living in the country." "You like living in the country." A shadow—it was nothing more swept over the clear brow. "I don't know—some day I hope to travel; but I am young still, and there is plenty of time. There is Drumabog, Mr. Lorraine." Inwardly, it is not improbable that Vincent Lorraine consigned Drumabog to a remote Eastern region, but aloud he observed—

div.head: CURRENT POLITICS.
div.p: CURRENT POLITICS.
GENERAL NEWS.
THE NEW BISHOP OF SODOR AND MAN.—Archdeacon Bardsley, of Liverpool, has been appointed Bishop of Sodor and Man. _ .

Saturday last was the anniversary of Waterloo. There are still a few veterans with us who took part in the sanguinary fighting on that fateful Sunday in June, IE/5. Pope Leo XIII. has appointed the Rev. C. Hariog, ton Moore, M.A., Christ Church, Oxford, administrator of the Pro-Cathedral, Kensington, to be one of his Privy Chamberlains. The Rev. Edward Martin Chapman, rector of Low Foynton, near Horncastle, was, seized with apoplexy while conducting service on Snnday night. He was removed home and died soon afterwards. . _

Arrangements are being; made for the holding of a general conference of shipowners in London in opposi- tion to the Transfer bf Registry Bill and the bill provid- ing for the compulsory annual survey of the boilers of steamers. DETERMINED SUICIDE.—A young man named Pettit, a baker, of Huntingdon, committed suicide on Saturday by jumping in front of the Leeds express from the plat- form of the Great Northern Station at Huntingdon. His body was carried some distance and literally cut to pieces. Another accident happened on the railway, pear Leicester, on Saturday. A labourer, 80 years ofPage, named Thomas Porter, was sent with some milk to Ashley Station, and by some means he got near a wall during shunting operations, and was crushed to death by the engine. A serious accident occurred at Stockport, on Monday, in connection with the Jubilee celebrations. Some salutes were being fired in honour of the occasion, and at Port- wood an old cannon burst, the fragments striking a young man, named Andert on,who was shockingly injured about the lower part of the body. He was taken to the Infirmary, where he now lies. The Committee on the Trade Marks and Designs Act of 1883 met on Saturday, at the Board of Trade. Lord Herschel! presided; and there were present the Earl of Crawford, Lord Alacnagliten, and Mr. James F. Hutton. The witnesses examined were Mr. H. Reader Lack, of the Board of Trade, and Mr. d'Andria, manufacturer, of Stockport, on headings as trade marks. Tne lamest single cotton spinning mill in Bolton, called the Jubilee Mill, belonging to Messrs. John Mus- grave and Sons. Limited, and which is to contain 90,000 spindles, has advanced to the fourth floor, though the first brick was laid so recently as March last. The lower floors are being rapidly completed, so that machinery can be worked before the roof is finished. The buildings are very substantial, and all fireproof. POLICE JURISDICTION 'AT THE MANCHESTER EXIILM- TION.—In an appeal on Monday in London against the conviction of a Manchester city police constable, on an information issued against him by Colonel Moorsom, the chief constable of the county, for refusing to leave the Exhibition building at Old Trafford when ordered to do so, the Court quashed the conviction, thereby establish- ing the right of jurisdiction over the building claimed by the city police force. TIIE TITHE WAR IN WALES: THF, OXFORD ULTIMATUM. —Saturday's report from the Meifod Valley, Mont- gomeryshire, states that the au thorities.of Christ Church College, Oxford, have written further, declining to grant the tithe abatement of 10 per cent, demanded by the farmers, and adding that, if no arrangements can be made for a peaceable settlement, they will be compelled to claim sufficient protecti m to enable them to recover their legal right without danger to the lives of those em- Ployed by them. THE GrLASGOW EXPLOSION: TILE FIRST. DEATH.— James Brown, aged seven, who was the most seriously injured in the canister explosion at Partick, on Friday, died in the Glasgow Western Infirmary, at 7 a.m. on Saturday, after terrible suffering. Doubt is expressed as to the recovery of several other of the victims. Eighteen children in all were injured, but in some cases only slightly. Col. Majendie, one of her Majesty's in- spectors of explosives, telegraphed to Glasgow, on Saturday, for full particulars of the Partick canister explosion. The canister now appears to have been a ship's distress signal. FRATRICIDE IN LIVERPOOL.—A fatal quarrel occurred at Liverpool on Saturday night between two labourers named Golding (brothers), living in Sterne-street. The two were playing cards with another man named Roberts, and all v ere under the influence of drink. The Geldings quarrelled, Martin calling his brother John a cheat. After a short altercation the former rose from his seat, called out he was stabbed, and fell to the ground. John Golding ran away to a friend, to whom lie said he had stabbed his brother, and requested him to go to the house to see how the injured man was. He then left, and was not apprehended until five o'clock on Sunday morning, when he was found by the police in a lodging-house. The injured man was taken to the Royal Infirmary, but died immediately after admission. ANOTHER LETTER FROM MR. H. M. STANLEY.— Mr. F. de Winton sends to the newspapers a copy of a long letter from Mr. H. M. Stanley, dated Stanley Pool, April 26. It describes some of the difficulties with which Mr. Stanley has had to contend. The flotilla under his command must (Mr. Winton says) move slowly, and will take from forty to fifty days in ascending the Congo. This would time Mr. Stanley's arrival at the Biyerre, where lie proposed to make an entrenched camp, about the 10th of this month; and he has now probably com- menced the laud journey of 350 miles which separates him from the Albert Nyanza and Emin Pasha. It is pos- sible the steamers may return in time to catch the Portuguese mail of July, in which case there may be news of the expedition about the middle of August; but it is most probable that nothing will be heard from them till about the 15th of September.

TILE NEW COINKGE.—On Monday morning, the Bank of England commenced the issue of the new coinage, for which is very lar 'e number of applications have been received from London and provincial bankers. The amount of the issue is as yet indeterminate, and the bank will go on supplying until the demand falls off. Applicants, however, do not r ceive all they ask for, but generally about one-third, as the amount coined so far is not very large, and there is a large stock iof old coins n hand at the Mint. Coins of eyery denomination were issued on Monday, including the double florin, for which there is a good demand, and the £5 piece. There is an idea that these latter coins are not intended for circulation. This is not so. Naturally, the number struck will be limited,but they will circulate quite as legally as any other coin of the realm, although no doubt in lst of them will find their way to the cabinets of ,numismatists, or be otherwise kept as mementoes of the Jubilee year. A SUPPOSED DYNAMlTER.—Considerable sensation was created in Birmingham on Monday by the circumstances divulged at a coroner's inquest upon a man unknown, whose body was found in the canal at Small Heath on Saturday morning with the throat cut. In his pocket was found a pocket-book containing several receipts for explo- sive mixtures, an address at New York, and a number of entries of sums of money received or paid. The conjecture was formed that the deceased was an emissary of the dyna- mite party told off for work in connection with outrages, but that becoming afraid he cut his throat and jumped into the canal. An examination of the book shows that

the receipts are for mixtures for cartridge fulminates, one of them having the word " Boxer" preceding it, and being the mixture for the Boxer cartridge. The address of Rooke's Paper Mills is also among the entries, and proves to be that of the maker of the paper used for cartridge making at a well-known local ammunition factory. The body has been photographed to assist identification. The police state that they attach no sig- nificance to the discovery, but the recent, Home Office circular and other information has set them on the alert. Tan HEROINE OF GIRTON COLLEGE.—The great Classical Tripos which was published at Cambridge on Saturday morning was remarkable for the success attained by a Girton student. The tow, Miss Ramsay, beat all the male students, she being the only one of either sex to bass in the first division. Miss Agnata Francis Ramsay, of Girton College, who has ob- tained the highest place in the first class of the Cambridge Classical Tnpos this year, is the third daughter of Sir James H. Ramsay, of Banff, N.B. Miss Ramsay was born in January, 1867, and was educated at home until October, 1880, when she entered St. Leonard's School, St. Andrews, N. 8., where she remained till she obtained a scholarship at Girton in 1884. She began to study Greek in 1883, her teachers at St. Leonard's in that subject and in Latin being Miss E. Case and Miss Clark, both certifi- cated students of Girton College. Miss Ramsay's father, Sir James Ramsay, was distinguished at Oxford, where he took a double first. The present Professor of Latin in the University of Glasgow is her uncle, and her great uncle, who preceded him in that chair, was the author of Ramsay's " Roman Antiquities." A MAD BULL IN LONDON.—TWELVE PERSONS INJURED. —A bull, which, so far as is at present known, injured at least twelve persons, caused great excitement in Poplar on Sunday. About half-past nine o'clock two policemen had their attention called to a bull which was running along the East India Dock Road in the direction of the docks, followed by a large crowd. It made a rush at a woman, who was with her three children, and knocked her down, breaking one of her arms. One of the chil- dren also received a severe scalp wound and other injuries. The bull then made its way into the East India Docks, where it, knocked down a policeman. From the docks the bull rushed towards the Poplar Hos- Vtal, and on its way threw over a pony which was attached to a cart in which six persons were seated. It then tore wildly along towards Aberfeldie-street and overthrew two tramway horses. A constable then managed to drive the bull on to a piece of vacant ground; but it got away and rushed into Benleader- street, and attacked a van and also a cart. The anitm then ran its horns into a dog and tossed it over a : wall. In Leven's-road a woman was tossed and severely injured, Constable Wallett then obtained a rifle, but being tor- excited to use it himself, handed it to a Mr. Marsh, who fired two shots, but with no effect. The rifle was then handed to Mr. Gould, who fired two shots, one of which struck the bull in the head and brought him to the ground. Altogether, about twelve persons were treated at the Poplar Hospital for injuries received from the infuriated beast. Later on the carcase of the bull was claimed by a slaughterman of Aldgate market, who stated that about nine o'clock that morning two bulls broke away. He succeeded in killing one, but the other got away. •

Fifty years elapsed since her sovereignty commenced, and great were the rejoicings when her grandfather entered oO his Jubilee, seventy-eight years since, the cererno- kat yr,ai eay was of a far more imposing kind than any wat then marked the occasion, while the wealth of pop- acclaim was even more in evidence. For months, Parations for the great ceremony of thanksgiving in Westminster Abbey had been proceeding, and within Past week they had been pushed on with the • 4., teat vigour. • b M HYDE PARK CORNER TO WATERLOO-PLACE. irk ra s„:0411,1 Corner, even at the early hour of nine in th. g, Presented a' remarkable appearance. Long •Ziasel crowds of spectators had been converging `v4 Caei„alld by that hour the vast open space be- " unke of Wellington's archway and the

graceful columns that attest the genius of Decimus Burton, was densely packed with people. A more stately sight than that presented for fully two hours before the Royal procession itself passed it would be difficult to imagine. Apsley House, St.. George's Hoi- pita!, and the palatial residences in Grosvenor. .ace and Piccadilly were all splendidly decorated, and never before did the historic corner look more bright alld animated. Opposite Ansley House the crowd was so ponderr's that inch by inch the line marking the mute was momentarily contracted. The police and Military, despite all their desperate efforts, had to yield ground, and the auth4ri- ties had to resort to the expedient of bringing up the Hussars, who were told to. back theis steeds on the surging crowd. The order was promptly obeyed, though with as little violence as possible, and the manceuvre thoroughly succeeded. The people wen, forced back, and the line remained intact. . The inevitable effect o: this awful crushing, combined with the intense heat ca the sun, was that many persons in the crowd faihted, and when extricated had to be taken away on stretchers. Equally severe wee the pressure hi Ergent-street and it Waterloo-place, where the crowds were enortnons. Here, too, the nurriberS proved too great for the police ard infantry to cope with, and a squadron a Boots Greys had to 'be ordered up to keep the populace ir. check. At half-past ten the Dula. A nd.Duchess of Teck, who had previously driven to Buckingham Palaeo from tyrosvertor-place, started for the Abbey in com- pany with the Hereditary Prince Frederick of Art- hault and Prince Ernest of Saxe Meiningem and escorted by Life Guardsmen. They were succeeden ~ in a few minutes by a processsion Of Royal and distin- guished personages from the Alexandra Hotel, including SiameSe and Persian Princes, the Prince Romatu of Japan and Queen Kapiolani of Hawaii. Just before eleven another of the Royal processions passed through the archway at Constitution Hill and emerged into Piccadilly amidst a scene of great enthusiasm. No less than 15 carriages were included in the long procession, and amongst the occupants who came in for the heartiest greeting were the King of ' Denmark, the King and Queer. of Belgium, the King of Greece, and the Ring of Saxony. . There was a considerable lapse of time before the Queen's procession left the palace, and the excitement in the meantime had become intense. At twenty minutes to twelve the distant sound of cheering from the direction or Buckingham Palace indicated that the Royal procession Nut started. A few minutes after the glittering cavalcade appeared upon the scene. The cheers were loud and hearty as the Crown Prince of Germany and the three sons of the Queen went by on horseback, but the enthusiasm of the crowd knew no bounds when her Majesty her- self appeared in company with the Princess of Wales and the Crown Princess of Germany. Alike from house- tops and from street cheer succeeded cheer, the bands struck up the National Anthem, and the ovation ac- corded to her Majesty WAA one such as she can never have experienced before. The sight that presented itself as the stately. procession made its way slowly along PiccarlillAwas one never to be forgotten. and this scene of loyal erithusiasm only grew in interest as her Majesty and her imposing escort progressed down Regent-Street.
WATERLOO-PLACE TO TRAFALGAR- SQUARE, .

The appearance of Waterloo-place was truly magnifi- cent, the decorations partaking of all colours of the rain- bow. intermingled with floral displays in all their sum- mer loveliness. The new and palatial buildings of white stone in Pall Mall provided a striking background, the whole completing a picture extremely effective. The soft easterly breeze which gratefully tempered the heat of the sun, caused the myriads of flags and festoons to gaily flutter, creating a most animating and pleasing sight. The eye, becoming dazzled by the gorgeous colours, wandered in vain in search of one vacant millet. In all directions the visi3n ranged over garlands of the choicest flowers, and multitudes of human beings. Not only were the fronts of mansions and clubs hidden with gaily-decorated stands, -which provided accommodation- for thousands, but almost every roof was crowded with loyal sightseers, chiefly in holiday attire. The Jimior Carlton Club was one MISS of flags and festoons, the names of most of the colonies comprised in the. British Empire being set out in gold letters on a crimson back- ground. The Carlton Club, on the opposite side of Pall Mall, was nearly hidden behind range above range of flowers in full bloom; and many other buildings in " Clubland " displayed similar tokens of -loyalty and welcome. A .magnificent triumphal arch spanned the southern end of Regent-street, reaching far above the highest build- ings, and forming one of the most conspicuous objects along the route of the royal procession. It was sur- mounted by the Crown anclUe Royal Standard, under- neath being a large medallion portrait of her Majesty, with the words, in large gold letters, "Victoria, our Queen." Shortly before the arrival of the first of the royal carriages, an alarming incident occurred. An officer's charger became restive, owing no doubt to the great excitement, and before its rider could control it. the noble beast galloped off from the direction of Trafalgar -square. and made for Pall Mall. The young naval officer displayed great coolness and endeavoured to rein in his horse. The crowds imme- diately opened, but unfortunately a moment ,to late, one lady being knocked down and many others severely injured. Owing to the great crnsh, the horse was stopped as it was about to turn up Regent-street, and, with its rider still mounted, was led back to the place whence it belted, the officer being loudly cheered for his Plucky conduct by the vast multitude. Fortunately this was the only serious mishap which occurred between the two points we are now deseribing. The injured lady had meanwhile been carried away by the ambulance staff, who really seemed übiquitous, and the people soon re- gained the position near the line of soldiers which they had hastily deserted, and lost all recollection of their fears by an amusing incident which occurred between the police and some daring spirits among the "youth of England." Several young fellows had managed to climb, unobserved, to the top of the pedestal which is surmounted by the equestrian statue of George 111., in Waterloo Place. They, were not, how- ever, allowed to occupy such a favoura.bie spot, as two policemen proceeded. amidst the laughter and cheers of the crowd, to climb the pedestal for the purpose of dis- lodging the interlopers. The latter were. apparently in no frame Of mind to give in, and an amusing and lively game, of "hide and seek" ensued between the bronze legs of one of England's dead kings and those of his horse. The game would have lasted some considerable time, to the infinite amusement of .the spectators, had not other policemen, who had„come to the assistance of their com- rades. dragged the intruders ignominiously to tetra firma. The little incident pver, the good-natured crowd once more settled down` tO await the approach of Royalty. Their patience was soon to be rewarded, for at twenty-five mirfutes to eleven, the first car- riages in the procession emerged through the triumphal arch. The occupants. although almost hidden from view, the carriages being closed, were accorded a hearty recep- tion. The Indian chiefs and deputations were greeted with loud cheers as they passed along the route. The other Royal personages came in for a share of the enthu- siasm, but the climax was reached when the Prince of Wales, riding a noble charger, and accompanied by his two brothers, the Dukes of Edinburgh and Connaught, and the sons-in-law, the grandsons, and grandsons-in- law of her Majesty preceded the Queen. As the Queen and Empress passed through Waterloo-place and Cock- spur-street, her subjects cheered to the echo, and thou- sands of handkerchiefs were waved. Her Majesty never ceased to graciously bow in acknowledgment of such an outburst of loyalty, and seemed highly pleased with lv,r reception. The i.oute at Waterloo-place was kept by detachments of the Household ,Cavalry, Hussars, Royal Engineers, and polite ; but the people maintained the greatest decorum.

The scene inside the Abbey was one of, great magnifi- cence. Human ingenuity had been exhausted in contri:. buting to its splendour, and the result was a spectacle which called for the genius of a Turner to perpetuate it. The Abbey had been so transformed that it depended for a time on its topmost windows for light; so that while the most elevated of the gaily-dressed spectators and white-robed choristers were bathed in the glory of the. sunlight that played about the capitals of the clustered pillars and the groining of the vaulted roof, all below was in shadow that would have been sombre in its depth, but for the richness and variety of colour dis- played in the apparel of the assembled congregation. These contrasts of light and shade, seen within such a building, and on such an:occa.sion, heightened every de- signed effect, and rendered the scene one calculated to live in the memory for a lifetime. The doors of the Abbey were opened at nine o'clock. This, though suffi- ciently early for every-reasonable person, was net soon enough to satisfy the impatience of those people greedy of best places. Consequently the approaches to the Abbey resembled for about an hour a little too much the pit doors of a' popular theatre on an eagerly antici- pated "first night.", A .quirter of an hour had not, elapsed before every seat—except those reserved for the most exalted personages-.-was occupied. The people seated themselves and :gazed round with a sigh of relief. Many of them who had been watching the huge piles of timber that had been disappearing for weeks within the portals of the Abbey, had feared that the grand oPO face was being converted into a tawdry imitation of air opera house,and would not be recognisable; but the firstglance reassured them that the Abbey still preserved its indi- viduality.. It was dressed, but nPt masked. The tombs' and monuments of the illustrious dead were for the time hidden from view, but the awe-inspiring,, fratiires of the noble building were still to be beheld in all their dignity. The mass of crude timber had taken form as balconies and galleries in the aisles and transepts, and its raw whiteness had disappeared beneath a covering of mauve cloth and draperies of crimson, lopped up in rich folds. The huge galleries were supported by pillars and mas- sive beams, covered with white cloth—an ill-chosen colour, because of its looking, at a little distance, so like whitewash. div.head: 111 E EXAMINER. SATURDAY, JUNE 25, 18,7
div.p: 111 E EXAMINER. SATURDAY, JUNE 25, 18,7
THE THAMES EMBANKMENT TO THE HOUSES OF PARLIAMENT.

For purely spectacular effect there was probably no position from which the procession could be better viewed than a doign of 'vantage on the Thames Embank- ment. By nine o'clock the throng was so great that the police and the military commenced to block all ways of ingress, and the roadway under Charing-cross bridge speedily became blocked with a vast number of human beings. The first procession of any kind which rewarded their patience was that of the Lord Mayor and 100 other fully robed representatives of the city, 9! London, and afterwards the procession containing the Indian princes swept around the corner of Whitehall-place on to the Embaffirment. The 'second official procession, that of the foreign Royalties, came into view about noon. Immediately they had gone by the sound of distant cheering was wafted from Trafalgar-square, the troops lining the roadway were called to attention, and as the first mem- bers of the field officers' escort came down Northumber- land-avenue the long pent-up enthusiasm of the multi- tude found vent in a mighty cheer. The open carriages containing the young Princesses. grand-daughters of the Queen, were very heartily greeted, but when the escort of Princes, her Majesty's sous and grandsons, sons-in- law and grandsons-in-law, came in sight there was a a louder and longer outburst, special cheers being again and again given for the Crown Prince of Germany, who saluted repeatedly to right and left. But now arose a mightier cheer, which was echoed and re-echoed along the whole line of the embankment, for the Queen herself came in view. On the approach of her Majesty's car- riage there was an increased heartiness of cheering, together with the waving of' hats and handkerchiefs, and as the Queen passed along in front of the Palace of Westminster towards the Abbey thee demonstrations of loyalty wers repeated and even intensified. •

Westminster, 'in conferrinity with precedent, read the Lesson, which was taken from the First Epistle of St. Peter, chapter ii., and in doing so occupied the same place in front of the altar as the Primate had done in offering up prayer. Then followed the anthem, "Blessed be the Lima thy God, which delighted in thee." This composition, also from the pen of Dr. Bridge, was written especially for the Jubilee, and was first per- formed before the Queen in January last. After an opening allegretto movement, occurs a stately andante maestoso, into which, as an obligato for the organ, Dr. Bridge has ingeniously dove-tailed a few bars of the National Anthem. In the middle of the anthem is inserted, by phrmission of her Majesty, the chorale " Gotha," composed by .the late Prince Consort. The remainder of the ser- vice was conducted by the Archbishop of Canterbilry, the choral "Amen" to the Benediction being prolonged sufficiently to enable the congregation to join in silent prayer before the dying away of the strains from the organ. The ceremony at an end, the Primate returned to his seat at the northern end of the Communion table, and the Queen' rising from the Coronation Chair, signalled to thelleir Apparent to approach her. The Prince immediately stepped to her Majesty's side, and, making a low obeisance, kissed hands; the Queen kissing her son on the cheek before permitting him to depart. The Crown Prince of Germany next approached and kissed her Majesty's hand—an example followed by every other prince on the dais. In each case her Majesty returned the salute with a motherly kiss on the cheek or forehead. The Princesses on the left of the Queen, headed by the Crown Princess of Germany, and the Princess of Wales, then went through a similar cere- mony. The salutation of the first-named lady was remarkable for its warmth and 'heartiness, and the more remarkable in that just as her Royal Highness was about to retire, her Majesty called her back, and kissed her a second time. the Queen was preparing to leave the dais when she was obseived to look around, as though she had suddenly remembered something, and beckoning towards her the Grown Prince of Germany, on whom she had omitted to bestow the same mark of affection as on those who sub- sequently saluted her, she kissed him on both cheeks. Then her Majesty intimated to the Lord Chancellor that she was ready, and the return journey commenced, organist playing the "War March of the Priests" iu " Athalie ' (Mendelssohn), as the procession, in the same order as at the commencement of the proceedings, left the sacred edifice. The ceremony throughout was most solemn and impressive, and was followed by the closest attention by the Queen and those who sat around her on the dais. The Indian Princes, too, all or whom were furnished with books of the words, appeared to regard the service as one demand- ing their individual attention. The Royal and other invited guests were a considerable period in leav- ing the Abbey—an 'interval which was filled by the organist with selections of sacred music. As soon as the more distinguished personages had left, the specta- tors rapidly made their exit; and in less than an hour hardly a soul remained in the building. The ceremony lasted precis'ely an hour. During the earlier twarr nf the proceedings her Majeqtr. who was evidently .what fatigued after her ,i:ress from Buckingham Palace, remained seated; but wwards the close of the service she stood whenever the congregation did so.

div.head: OUTSIDE THE ABBEY.
div.p: OUTSIDE THE ABBEY.

The scene outside the Abbey, in Palace Square, and in the space known as the Broad Sanctuary, in front of the sacred edifice, was one which almost surpasses description. The appearance of the buildings and sides of the thoroughfares had, by the aid of carpenters, upholsterers, and decorators, undergone as complete a transformation as if they had been subjected to the influence of some genii of Oriental story. Numerous stands of great dimensions had been erected, and all were decorated with crimson cloth, trophies*of flags, and other ornamentations, and Royal Standards floated from the roofs of most of the buildings. Notwith- standing the large sums demanded for seats, they were all occupied from an early hour in the morning, among the occupants being many ladies in bright summer costumes. For those who had to be content with seeing what they could on font, there was very little standing room any- where near to the Abbey; but dense crowds assembled in the road facing Parliament-street, in Victoria-street, George-street, and adjacent thoroughfares. The route in the vicinity of the, Abbey was kept by a strong boily of police, and by the Grenadier Guards. Ticket-holders having allotted to them within the Abbey began to , as early as half-past o'clock, although the doors were not to be opened till nine; and for two hours there was a constant stream of arrivals of distinguished persons, inclu- ding a large number of Yeomen of the Guard, who, with a number of Gentlemen-at-Arms, took up a posi- tion inside a special pavilion, the entrance leading to a reception room which had beeu erected at the west f4ont of the Abbey, for the Queen to enter on her arrival. It was noticeable that the Gentlemen-at-Arms and other officers of the household wore black bands round their arms. Representatives of nearly every section of the British army kept arriving, and the bands whiled away the time of waiting by playing selections. Towards half-past ten o'clock the junior members of the Royal Family arrived in private carriages, and were con- ducted to their places within the Abbey. Their arrival was almost unnoticed by the spectators. In the mean- time, the Lord Mayor and representafives of the London Corporation had arrived, and entered the Abbey. Then came the eleven carriages containing the Indian chiefs and Aeputies of native Indian States, with their suites. They, however, did not attract the attention they. merited, from the fact that they were in closed carriages. Others of her Majesty's Royal guests soon afterwards arrived; and among them Queen Kapiolani of Hawaii, wearing a costume of the latest European fashion, came in for a good share of attention. It was nearly half-past eleven before there were any -signs of the approach of the Royal procession itself ; when the cheers given by the members of the House of Commons as her Majesty passed Palace Yard, were taken up by those on the stand near the Abbey. Then the bells of .St. Margaret's rang out a merry peal, and announcel to all at the Abbey that the royal pageant was 'approaching. The bands of the Life Guards and G renadiers in front of the AbbeYplityed the National Anthem, the thousands of spectators around the Abbey uncovered their heads, ladies waved their hand- kerchiefs; and amid tremendous cheering her Majesty frequently bowing her acknowledgement, drove urn° the entrance at the west front of the Abbey. It was twenty-five minutes to one when her Majesty alighted from the royal carriage. She was received by the high officers of state, and at once conducted into the reception room prior to her entrance into the Abbey.

div.head: INSIDE THE ABBEY.'
div.p: INSIDE THE ABBEY.'

Lar"MTh r feature which mark the Eastern potentate or noble. • '•ove all, they showed that they knew how to walk Nv dignity. ' They attracted, apart from their glittering diamonds, much admiration, and the two ladies of the party—the Maharani of Ruch-Behar and the Kanwarani Harnani Singh, who accompanied their husbands—were very favourably regatded for their sweetness of expression and grace of manner. The Peers assembled in their own House, and entered the Abbey in procession, headed by the Lord Chancellor, attended by his train-bearer. They were accompanied by their wives and peeresses in their own right, the tout ensemble being of a most brilliant character. On taking his seat, Lord Halsbury had on his right the• Prime Minister, wearing the Order of the Garter' the Marchioness of Salisbury, Lord and Lady Cade- gan, Lord Stanley of Preston, and the Irish Lord Chancellor (Lord Ashbourne). Other peers present were Earl Sutton, Earl Fortesque, and Lord St. Oswald. On the opposite side of the dais sat the members of the House of Commons, who commenced to assemble before nine o'clock, and in an hour the seats allotted to the Lower House presented an animated ap- pearance. Sir J. Mc.Garel-Hogg and Mr. Bolster-Booth, two of the new Peers, whose elevation had been an- nounced this morning, received the congratulations of their brother members, this probably being the last occa- sion on which they would sit as commoners. The major portion of those already assembled wore uniform, either court, military, naval, or volunteer; and it was sur- prising how few members of the People's House contented themselves with the ordinary walking coat. The Speaker, wearing his full-bottomed wig and his, State robes, and preceded by the Deputy-Sergeant, bear- ing the mace, entered the Abbey at eleven o'clock, and was followed by a considerable number of Privy Coun- cillors and others. On his right sat the Chairman of Committees (Mr. Courtney), Mr. Gladstone, the Home Secretary, the Secretary for War, the Chancellor of the Ex- chequer, the Chief Secretary for Ireland, and Mr. Mun- della. On his left were the kirst Lord of the Treasury, the Secretary for the Colonies, the First Lord of the Admiralty, the President of the Local Government Board, Mr.. Childers, Sir Wm. Harcourt, and the Post- master-General. The officers of the House sat imme- diately behind the Speaker, with Dr. Lyon Playfair, Mr. Shaw-Lefevre, the Lord Advocate, the Solicitor- General, Sir Henry James, and Mr. John Morley, who sat beside the Chaplain of the House, and in close proximity to his political chief. The Chief Com- missioner of Works was not far removed from two junior members of the Ministry. Lord Charles Beresfid and Colonel King-Harman who, sitting side by si , presented a brilliant contrast; the former displaying s full naval dress, and the latter a gorgeous military uni- form and trappings. Long after all had taken their places, and as the second procession marched up the nave at a quarter-past twelve, Lord Hartington came in, hot and dusty, having apparently had to run the gaunt- let of the immense :crowd outside. The noble lord was accommodated with a seat between Mr. Smith and Sir Henry Holland. The mace, which had been placed before the Speaker in the usual manner, was enveloped in red cloth as soon as the organ announced that the Queen had arrived at the west eutrance—the symbol of authority l•-'-o• for the nonce eclipsed in importance by the person., , ~,ence of the Sovereign in a building other than the House of Commons. The next persons of dis- tinction to arrive were the Duke and Duchess of Teck, the Hereditary Prince Frederick of Anhalt, and Prince Ernest of Saxe-Meningen. Shortly before eleven o'clock the first of her Majesty's guests arrived. They were headed, by the Persian, Siamese, and Japanese, and the Queen and Princess of Hawaii. The , princes were conducted • to the left of the sacrarium, and the ladies to the right. Immediately after them came a number of the German princes—fine, stalwart, soldier-like men.—in rich uniforms, and their breasts glittering with medals and stars. The Infanta Eulalia, of Spain, and the Crown Princess of Portugal quickly followed. After a considerable interval, another group of the Royal guests, whose appearance gave rise to no little curiosity on the part of the congregation, put in an appearance this company including such distin- guished reigning sovereigns as the Ring and Queen of the Belgians, the King of Saxony, the King of Denmark, and the King of ,Greece. They were followed by the Crown Prince of Austria—very resplendent in a white cuirassier uniform,—the Crown Prince of Portugal, the Crown Prince of Sweden, and the Crown Prince of Greece, who were all conducted to seats in the Sacrarium. At 12 30 the sound of cheering was heard, and four , minutes later a fanfare of trumpets announced her Majesty's entrance. At the same moment the National Anthem was commenced by the organist. The grand. 'Sons and grandsons-in-law of her Majesty headed the procession, the Grand Duke Liege of Prussia, who was In the front rank, being conspicuous by reason of his flowing uniform. The sons-in-law of the Queen, with the Crown Prince of Germany as the central figure, followed. The Crown Prince bore no traces of his recent indisposition. The Grand Duke of Hesse, another commanding figure in the group, also,attrabted con- siderable notice, and not a few remarked ori the appear- ance of Prince Henry of Battenburg for the first time in his uniform as Colonel of the Guards. The sons of the Queen came next, and then, preceded by the Lords Steward alai Chamberlain, with their wends, her Majesty bowing to right and left as' she noticed in the throng officers and ladies with whOm she is personally ae- quainted. Succeeding her Majesty came the Crown Princess of Germany and the Princess of Wales, hand-in- hand ; the former visibly affected. Then, two by two, walked the other daughters-in-law, grand-daughters, and grand-dau.ghters-in-law of the Queen. As her Majesty passed under the organ screen, the organist played Benedict's March from Handel's "Occasional uratoria." The Dean of Westminster, the -Bishop of London, and the Archbishops of Canterbury and York, who had gone with a body of minor and rcsidentiary canons to conduct her Majesty within the building, pro- ceeded to the Communion table, to be ready to begin the service., On reaching the dais, the Queen stopped and bowed three times to the distinguished, visitors around her, and . she was then handed by Lord Lathom to the Coronation chair, on which were laid her Majesty's robes of 'Slate. On her Majesty's right hand were thi% Prince of Wales and other Princes. To the immediate left was ,the Crown Princess of Germany, who wore a costume of mauve and black; next came the Princess of Wales, in a dress of cream-coloured silk, with a bonnet to match, trimmed with a bkinch of real roses; behind sat some eighteen more Princesses of "the Blood Royal, and the Mistress of the 14es. The last-named (the Duchess of Buccleugh) and the Duchess of Albany were the only ladies, besides her Majesty, who wore mourning; the other Princessess being attired in costumes of. the lightest and most. delicate Iffies— pkle blue, pale green, and pale pink predominating. The Queen wore a black costume, trimmed with lace, and a head-dress of white lace over diamonds. In the Sac- rarium, the dresses of the Queen of Hawaii and the Princes s Lililioltalani of Hawaii were the most con splenetic. The Infanta Eulalia, of Spain, who also sat in the Sacrarium. betrayed her nationality only by her head-dress—a kind of lace mantilla, worn over a dress of the palest pink.

THF; CEREMONY. • The Queen having taken her place in the Coronation 'chair—the second time in her life—and having.spent an interval in silent prayer, the service commenced; Canon Troutbeck intoning and the choir responding in an appeal to the Almighty on her Majesty's behalf. The efficiency and position of the choir were alike unique. Reinforced by picked voices from the Chapel Royal (Savoy), St. Paul's Cathedral, St. George's • Chapel (Windsor), the Chapel Royal (St. James's), and other homes of ecclesiastical musical .culture; the army of men and boys, under Dr. Bridge's command exceeded 250; and when contort and decorni joined to swell the volume of sound, the effect was soul-inspiring to a degree. As soon as the preliminary sentences were concluded, the organ- again pealed forth—this time itt more joyous Strain, the change from the closing minor chord of the' introduction to the spirited obligate in the natural key of, the Te Deum Laudamus, being grandly effective. By command of the Queen, the setting chosen for the To Deum was that by lO• -Royal Highness the Prince Consort. Then followed t be Lord's Prayer, intoned by the minor canon and the choir, after which the Archbishop of Canterbury, stepping to the front of the Communion table, read , the three special prayers which the Clergy had directed should be used throughout the country on Jubilee Day. The following was the first of these:—" Almighty God, we humbly offer unto Thy Divine Majesty.our prayers and hearty thanksgivings for our Gracious Sovereign Lady Queen Victoria, unto whom Thou hest accom- plished full fifty years of sovereignty. We praise . Thee, that through Thy grace she bath kept the charge Thou gayest her on the day when Thou didst set the crown upon ber head, bidding her to dojustice, slay the growth of iniquity, and protect the holy Church of God; to help and defend widows and orphans, to restore the things. cone to decay, maintain thethings that are restored, punish and reform what is amiss, and contirin what' is in good order, to keep the royal law and lively oracles of God. We bless Thee that Thou bast heard, through sorrow and through joy, our prayer that she should always possess the hearts of her people; and we humbly pray Thee, that for the years to come, she may rejoice in Thy strength, and at the resurrection of the just enterinto Thine immortal'kingdom, through Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen." During the reading of these and the other prayers anpointed for the day, the ma- jority of the foreign princes and princesses knelt, differ- ing somewhat irt this particular from the members of the English royal family, who, as a ule, followed the national custom of simply inclining their bodies forward. The Psalm chosen for the day was the 20th—" Exaudiat To Dominus :" The Lord hear thee in the day of trou- ble." The setting—the organist's own—was admir- ably calculated to display to the full the breadth of tone and fertility of resource of the well- trained choir. The first lined sung in unison by the full choir, gave the theme in its solemn simplicity. The decane and canton i then took up the melody alternately, the harmonic combinations varying with each line until, with. a fine Gregorian outburst, the first portion of the psalm was brought to a . close, with a rattle of drums and a flourish of trumpets. The second Part, "Rulers' Trust," maintaining the same melo- dic phrasing, was arranged as a choral duet for men .and boys, the "Gloria, Patti," being made the occasion of another Unisonic combination. The Dean of

div.head: RETURN BY WHITEHALL.
div.p: THE RETURN BY WHITEHALL.

On the return journey, the several processions, instead of proceeding by way of the Embankment, reached Trafalgar-square through the broad thorougbfare in which are situated the chief Government offices. Only those people occupying advantageous positions near the Trafalgar-square end could witness the procession to the Abbey as it crossed the sqyare to Northumberland- avenue. Every window and housetop, however, was occupied with gaily dressed people. Several fine stands had been erected at convenient points. The time of wait- mg was relieved in the first instance by the arrival of the military and naval detachments which lined the route. The Middlesex Artillery Volunteers were stationed in Bridge. street and Parliament-street, the Honouranle Artillery Company were outside the Treasury Buildings, and men of the Boyal Navy were placed outside the Admiralty and up to Trafalgar-square. After a few more tunes from the bands in the street, the advanced guards of the royal procession appeared. By this time the thorough- fare was crammed, people who had witnessed it in other parts of the route earlier having crowded through into Trafalgar-square. The people cheered her Majesty. In the interval between the first passage of the procession and the- return, a fresh formation was made of the troops and police, in order to keep the new route clear at the head of Whitehall. The people, however, were perfectly o, deny. As her Majesty appeared at the head of the square the band of the Royal Marines again played the National Anthem, while the boys of the Greenwich Naval School created a pretty effect by waving their hats. The procession was now in inverse order, the Queen's procession coming first. In a short time after the Royal party had passed, the troops were marched off, and the great crowd in the square dispersed in an orderly manner, through Pall Mall and St. James's. Coming into Pall Mall, the Queen was enabled to see the magnificent tributes of love and loyalty which had been prepared to greet her. Pall Mall itself was a veritable Fairyland, the long vista being one mass of festoons and bannerets, and as her Majesty passed the various clubs she was greeted with enthusiasm. Passing into Pall Mall the Queen was wel- comed by a huge banner of crimson, edged with gold, and inscribed "Victoria Regina et Imperatrix." At the War Office, which had been tasteful'y deeorated, the Queen met with a very hearty reception, flu.• enthusiasm reaching its highest point as her Majesty passed Marl- borough House, the square between which and the old St James's Palace contained many thousands of people. The Prince of Wales as he passed his London mansion again came in for a Jarge share of popular enthusiasm. The;Queen's procession turned out of Pall Mall into St. James's-street amidst rounds of cheers and waving of handkerchiefs. Nowhere during this memorable 'da'y were the crowd more dense than in St. James's-street on her Majesty's return. St. James's-street itself was decked out in the mokt marvellous' fashion. From top to bottom the street was alive with bunting, triumphal arches, banners, and crimson-covered balconies, while even the housetops were lined with spectators. Her Majesty smilingly bowed right and left. The scene viewed from Hyde Park corner, wet; grand in the extreme. The return journey along Piccadilly to Hyde Park Corner was only a repetition of what had occurred at the same spot earlier in the day. One of the most interesting features in the return journey so far as ,Constitution Hill was the reception accorded to her Majesty by the school children. This evidence ofjuvenile loyalty seemed to afford her Majesty considerable delight. The Queen reached Buckingham Palace upon her return from the Abbey at twenty minutes to three, after having been absent for nearly three hours and a half. She looked none the worse for her long and fatiguing journey. Her Majesty, we ascertained, was not very much fatigued after the exertions she had gotie through, and expressed her gratification at the completeness with which the arrangements for the ceremonial had been carried out.

div.head: ROYAI BANQUET.
div.p: ROYAI BANQUET.

----•— - - In the evening her Majesty gave a grand banquet t 6 her Royal guests. Sixty-four Royal personages were entertained in the Queen's room, Ind covers were laid for 132 members of the Royal household. At half-past ten the Queen held a reception. THE ILLUMINATIONS. .

The West End of London was all ablaze a, t night with illuminations. The crowds which filled the streets during the greater portion Of, the day re-assembled as the shades of evening fell and seemed to grow even larger as the time for lighting up arrived. The •display at Marl- borough [louse, the residence of tam Prince of Wales, took as its motto "God Save the Queen." There was a remarkable display of electric lights at the Junior Carlton. Lord Salisbury's private residence. in Arlington-street had a'display of its own, and :di the foreign embassies and legation exhibited a specisl device. Although the display of illurninatiors in the city was not as general as it has been upon some previous occasions of great national rejoicing, it was so brilliant in some respects as to bear fair comparison with those even more widely spread. The great centre of attraction Was the great open space which is surrounded by the Mansion House, the, Bank of England, the Royal „Exchange, the Union Bank of London, and the offices of the Liverpool and London and Globe Insurance Company, for each Of those buildings was alpine of brilliaticy.'The huge columns of the Mansion House were snaked'" with thousands of gas lamps, while above them all hung a transparency, with the motto "God guard our Queen.' Right opposite is the long and comparatively low facade of the Bank of .Englandovhere a great effect was Made by a mytiad of parti-coloured gas lamps, hung in festoons, with occasional stars and crystal devices. The splendid facade of the Royal Exchange offered even a finer field for the illuminating decorations, and it Was well taken advantage of, for in addition to a large device hung at a height in the Centre, thousands of oil lamps and gas jets were used to light up the columns, and to stamp the lines of the building in clear fire: Immense crowds of people thronged into the city from all parts to a 'late hour, and all the Main thoroughfares were so crowded that in some places they were almost impassable, but no serious mishap occurred.
INCIDENTS AND ACCIDENTS. SAD FATALATIES.

There were several accidents of a minor character attending the Jubilee celebrations in London, on Tuesday. Several liersons, including two soldiers, were treated for sunstroke. Many others who were crushed or over- powered by the heat were attended to by the Ambulance corps. The total number of casualties was, however, comparatively small. A later telegram says that several cases treated at ()haring Cross Hospital were of a serious descripton. k sailor, named Bennett, who was severely kicked by a horse in the chest, expired before the ambulance reached the hospital. There were also several pleb= .filuffering from epileptic attacks, On Tuesday morning, an alarming omnibus accident,by which several persons 'were severely injured and a number had narrow escapes, occurred outside King's Cross Railway' Station, London, About nine o'clock an

The Queen has been graciously pleased, on the occa- sion of her Majesty's Jubilee, to confer the dignity of an earldom upon Lord Londesborough. Her Majesty Was also been pleased to confer a peerage of the United Kingdom upon the Earl of Strathmore and Viscount Galway. Her Majesty further has been pleased to confer the dignity of a peerage upon each of the fol- lowing gentlemen :—Sir John St. Aubyn, Bart., M.P., Sir Wm. Armstrong, Sir James M`Garel Hogg, Right Hon. George Sclater Booth, M.P., E. Reßowes, Esq., H. Eaton, Esq., M.P. The Queen has also been pleased to confer the honour of Knight of the Garter (extra) upon H.I.H. the Crown Prince of Austria. The following gentlemen to be sworn members of the Privy Council :—John Floyer, Esq., and Sir .1. Cowell. Her Majesty has been pleased to confer the dignity of a baronetcy upon Sir A. H. .Macleod, Esq., Queen's Surgeon, Edinburgh; H. W. Parker, Esq., Presi- dent Incorporated Law Society; J. C. Cuthbertson, Esq., School Board, Glasgow; W. C. Long, Esq., Shef- field; A. Doulton, Esq.; S. Eldridge. Esq., Croydon; W. J. Farrer, Esq.,'High Bailiff of Westminster; Dr. Aitken, Netley Hospital; B. F. Bristowe, Esq., Q.C., Vice-Chan- cellor of the Duchy of Lancaster; J. Wright, Esq., late chief engineer of the navy; Alderman Lawrence; Andrew Maclean, Esq., Partick ; Thos. Storey, Esq., Lan- caster; John Smith, Racy, Derby; Arnold White, Esq.; I. C. Robinson, Esq., surveyor of pictures; George Martin Holloway, Esq.; the Lord Mayor of York, Lord Provost of Glasgow. the Mayors of Liverpool, Leeds, Sheffield, Bristol, Salford, Newcastle-on-Tyne, Portsmouth, Nor- wich, and Windsor. The Queen has been graciously pleased to give direc- tions for the following promotions in, and appointments to, the Most Distinguished Order ot St. Michael and St. George To be Ordinary Members of the First Class or Knights Grand CTOSS of the said Most Distinguished Order :—Sir Edward William Stafford, K.C.M.0., formerly for many years Prime Minister of New Zealand. A. Shippard, Esq., M.A., D.C.L., C.M.G., Administrator and Chief Magistrate Of British Bechuanaland; John William Akerman, Esq., Speaker of the Legislative Council of Natal; James Alexander Grant, Esq., M.D., of Ottawa, in the Dominion of Canada.' To be Ordinary Members of the Third Class or Com- panions of the said most distinguished order :—John Fitzgerald Burns, Esq., Colonial Treasurer of New South Wales; Major-general Edward Harding Stewart, Military Adviser to several of the Australasian Colonies; Wm.
