VIENNA, SUNDAY Ntenr.—A catastrophe which is con- stantly recurring in this eountry happened yesterday at a ferry near Ka'rasa in Hungary. A procession of 300 pilgrims entered one of the broad ferry boats by which the Danube is crossed in those parts. Altogether regard- less of the dangers inourred from the faulty construction of such boats the people crowd in until the edge nearly touches the water. In the present instance a violent 'storm arose soon after the pilgrims had left the bank. The women, packed in a dense crowd, became frantic' with fear, and in a few minutes the boatmen lost their ' oars and with them all c,ettrol over the vessel. It swayed about for a few moments, end then capsized. Before the catastrophe happened the priest conducting the pil- grimage blessed his flock, then jumped into the river, and swam to shore. Of the 300 persons very few were able to save themselves. The bodies are being recovered. and the banks of the river in those parts present a ghastly spectacle, with 200 corpses laid on the grass. VIENNA, MONDAY non r.—The details of the catas- trophe on the Danube, by which so many persons have perished, are most heartrendMe. The ignorance and superstition of the people added' to the terrors of the scene, and the selfish and unreasoning manner in which numbers scrambled into the small boats which put off from the shore to save them increased the magnitude of • the disaster. In many instances those who were trying to save others lost their own lives. The priest who saved himself and a child by swimming has since died. A fragment of the Virgin's flog, Wilier/ was carried at the head of the processien, floated to the shore, and will be preserved as a memorial of the dreadful day. One woman lost three young daughters, and in numbers of families as many as 10 persons have been drowned. It is now said tlett as many as 400 persons' were in the boat, be- sides two carts and four horses. one woman saved her- self by bolding on to the tail of a horse which swam to the shore with her. The dead lie in long rows on either bank of the Danube, and their faces, which are much contorted, show the terrible struggle they went through before succumbing. Those who come to identify their dead can scarcely bear the ordeal through which they have to pass before they discover the bodies for which .they are searching... BUDA-PEWIT, SUNDLY.-.--Whlst the elections were in pro- gress at Matterdorf, yesterday, the gendarmerie were attacked by a crowd of Croaiion electors. In defence, they shot seven of their antagonists, killing five • and seriously, wounding two. The gendarmerie, on their side, had two of their me.r.bers injured. In consequence of this outbreak the elections were suspended locally. BUDA-PESTYI, MONDAY.—The progress of the elections is watched with the greatest anxiety by the authorities, , in consequence of the threatened anti-Jewish outbursts. At Dunaszerahely, last night, after the election of Szabo, the anti-Semitic candidate, the mob set lire to the Jewish quarter of the town, totally destroying it. Eighty houses were destroyed, the ocetipants, to the number of 120, all Jewish families, losing all their possessions.

THE QUEEN'S LITTLE SUBJECTS, AND WHAT THEY THINK OF HER. The Editor of "Little Folks" Magazine having asked children under• ten years of age to tell him what they thought about the Queen, gives in the July number the following account of the response to his invitation:— Almost all the letters---and I have ' been simply delue,ed with epistles—were capital, many of them admirable. Little folk under ten have the daring of their years. They are all friendly to the Queen. They nAtnit the grandeur of her position, but they do not Stan in such awe of it as competitors of an older growth. They all declare that they "love her." They are sure, too, that She is "good and clever." One tells MP that she goes to - the cottages of the poor and talks with them, "which shows "—so the moral is drawn—" she is not at all proud... although she is grand and great?! Another relates the number of times she has been shot at without harm "because she asks God to take care of her." A third . informs me that in their family circle even the baby can sing "God save the Queen." Several have been im- mensely pleased with her conduct to her dog "Dash" after the Coronation. "I never saw the Queest, as she never conies to Ireland, where I live," is the preface of a,. highly laudatory letter, the writer of which of course means that her Majesty has not been in Ireland since he was born. That Is a matter, however, which may yet be put right. A. little lad informs me that his mother has told him that rill "true boys love the Queen, and he wants to be a' true boy." But the most tremendous token of goodwill that has readied me i•nmes from a little fellow who hopes that the Queen "will live another fifty years."

_ passenga.s. for 1 lie-Ainwe—pro,...,4lon, when the wheels unaccountably became fixed in the tram lines. and the 'bus overturned, the occupants being thrown violently to the ground. Four persons had to be taken to the hospital; but the remainder were treated on the spot. - - -

On inquiry at the hospitals after the procession, we learn that the procession was marred by some very sad and serious casualties. At Charing Cross Hospital it wag reported that a man named Geo. Bennett, of Lille-terrace, Addison-road, Euston House Estate, had been killed by a kick in the chest from a horse. A very serious case of fracture of.the skull of a man unknown by falling about 14ft. from a lamppost had also been admitted. Between fifty and sixty minor casualties, such as simple fractures, &c., had been treated. At St. Thomas's Hospital only one case, that of a boy who had injured himself by falling from a tree in Hyde Park, was reported. There were a few cases at St. George's Hospital, but one was a very sad one. A man named Joseph Camerford (37), address not known, fell from a scaffold while the procession was passing Groevenor Place, and sustained fatal injuries. At Middlesex Hospital no person was treated during the progress of the procession, but later in the afternoon a man, name unknown, but believed to reside at Kentish Town, was admitted suffering from severe injuries to the head, caused by his stumbling from a pavement in New Bond-street and in falling striking his head against the 'wheel of a passing cab. It is reported that he has since succumbed.

div.head: WEDNESDAY'S PROCEEDINGS.
div.p: WEDNESDAY'S PROCEEDINGS.

The Queen received visits in Wednesday from a large number of distinguished persons at Buckingham Palace. Afterwards she held a recoption, at which she was formally presented with Jubilee gifts from foreign Courts, from her Colonies, from various localities within the United King- dom, and from 'the women of England." The contribu- tors to the last-named gift are said to number over 3 000 000 On Wednesday the address by which it is accompanied was handed to her Majesty. The gift itself is to be In the form of an equestrian statue of the late Prince Consort, the foundation for which will be laid by the Queen neat month. Over £75,000 has been subscribed, and t'. ere is expected to be a surplus for some charitable pur- pose. The deputation of lidies included many persons of high rank, and numbered altogether about 150. Her Majesty is stated to have made a gracious reply to the ad- dress. Her Majesty left for Windsor in the evening, driv- ing en route through Hyde Park, where about 30,000 chit- 4ren had been massed and sang the National Anthem. Westminster Abbey was crowded during the afternoon, when the Jubilee Thanksgiving Service was repeated, and solos were song by Madame Nordica. The service was for the benefit of the London hospitals.

div.head: FOREIGN CELEBRATIONS.
div.p: FOREIGN CELEBRATIONS.
BERLIN, TrumpAv.—A special service in commemora- tion of the Queen's Jubilee was held in the English church here to-day. The Emperor sent his congratula- tions to the British Ambassador.

VIENNA, TIIESDAT.—The Jubilee was celebrated here to-day. 'r' Imbassador gave a grand banquet. Sr. Prri...,sUßO, TIIESDAY.—The Journal de St. Peters- bourg says :—To-day all civilised nations unite their congratulations and good wishes to those of the British people. Eons, Tunsnsy.—To-day's paper's publish leading articles upon Queen Victoria's Jubilee;referring to her Majesty in terms of the warmest eulogy. GIBRALTAR, THESDAY.—The Jubilee festivities Com- menced to-day with a thanksgiving service at the Spanish Cathedral. MADRID, TUESDAY.—The English residents gave a Jubilee dinner last evening. LIMA, Toxs-DAT.—The British commercial houses closed to-day, in honour of the Jubilee. VALPARAISO, TUESDAY.—Queen Victoria's Jubilee was celebrared here yesterday with great rejoicing. MELBOBRNE, TIIESDAY.—The celebration of the Queen's Jubilee was held to-day with great enthusiasm. PESTH, TUESDAY.—AII the newspapers to-day publish sympathetic articles on Queen Victoria's Jubilee. WIESBADEN, TITICSDAY.—A splendid garden party in honour of Queen Victoria was given in Kur Park yester- day. There were rejoicings also at Homburg. '

NEW YORK, SATURDAY.—Another daring robbery of s. train is reported to-day. The .robbery occurred on amt. east-bound train on the Southern Pacific Railroad near Schulenburg. The robbers, who were seven in number., succeeded in carrying off about 10,000dols. worth of' plunder, half beingtalien from the passenger care ant half from the mail and express cars.

NEW YORK, SirrmAy.--twentyive thousand members of the organised labour party, with their sympathisers, held a Mass m eting in Union-square last night, to do honour to Father M'Grlynn, and to protesragainst the manner in which the Paiial e has treated him. After, Father M'Glynn had made a speech, resolutions were passed expressing aepreval of the course which he had taken in his defiance IA the Church.

"CLEARING OUT" EENTUCKIAN DESPERADOES NEw Yoga, THURADAY.—A despocb from Morehead Kentucky, 'announces that the Sheriff's posse at that place has killed four desperadoes, after a most determined resist- ance. They were the last of a gang which had infested the. district f r two years past, daring which fifteen person were killed in vendetta warfare. .
GERMANY.-ARREST OF A DEPUTY.--
RAILWAY DISASTER

The session of the German Parliament was closed oft , Saturday by an Imperial Message, in which the deputies were assured of the Empi.,ror's approbation of their dili- gent and faithful labour "in promotiag the welfare of. the country and assuring peace." The bulletins with regard to the Einper,r are very guarded, and the neces- sity of "Crest care" is enforced. Herr li:raker, a Socialist.member of the German Par- :iament, was arrested at the moment when he was leaving the Parliament House in Berlin after the conclusion ot the session.

BERLIN, MONAlr.—Yesterclay evening, a train from Potsdam ran into a train which was standing still at the Wandset Station. The engine of the moving train was thrown on its side, and the burning coal set fire to one of the carriages of the other train, and the car was itnme- diately enveloped in flames. The occupants were speedily rescued, but two persons are reported dead, and five seriously injured. The actual extent of the disaster has ' not yet been ascertained. Some persons who were In the carriage are missinv nut GERMAN EMPEROR. _ _ _ _

• Car light weight champion of Eng- land, men,j oi f mßm Birmingham, Mitchell, of Philadelphia, light weight: champion of America, early on Saturday, at an obscure point on the Sound. 30 miles from 'New York. There were only 47 spectators present, each of whom had paid 100 dollars for.adtni-ssion to see the fight. Both men 'were in splendid condition, and had been well trained. • Carney at about his usual weight. Mitchell, the. champion, is 25 years of age, stands sft. Bin. ainmudgewrhiteciagn hedl33 lbs. on going into the scale yesterday. The men showed icience rarely witnessed in these encounters. They were well matched, but Carney's' powerful hitting wore his opponent down at the close. Altogether eleven rounds were fought, the combatants wearing "kid gloves," and the battle lasted 43 minutes. Both men showed smartness frotn the first., but Carney, breaking through Mitchell's defence, struck him sharply in the mouth, drawing, blond in the first rouna. Mitchell, however, fought with the utmost pluck, and, although he was severely punished, the victory wasi' extremely doubtful up to the end of the ninth round; and the Americana backed their man freely.

Jr! the tenth ro—u-n-cf,-6irney forced the fighting, and '• hitting with wEinderful vigou-r, grassed his man twice in the Same round. In the eleventh round, it was apparent; at tale outset that Mitchell was about pla)ed out. lie could make no stand, and was driven by Carney all over , the ring, and finally knocked down right over the ropes. The American charimion was then completely beaten. He: tried pluckily to rise twice at the call of " time ;" butt each time fell back again, and his second then threw up., the sponge. The umpire i mmediat<...y awarded to Carney the belt for the light weight. championship of the world., his supporters congratulating him heartily npon great fight he had won. The stakes amounted to 1,006! dollars, and 1,00.0 dollars of the gate money aLso goes toot the victor.

There are treats and treats. A large num- ber of persons have been " treated " at various hospitals for injuries received on Jubilee Day. They got more than they bargained for, and did not like it. The sad thing is that several lives have been lost. A sac•ifice of life seems inevitable on a national holiday; and we must accept the inevitable, or give up holidaying.

Widnes has not been able to bring itself to I formally celebrate the Jubilee. There was a meeting on the subject, but so many projects were mooted that nothing was done. Be- tween half a-dozen stools the Widnes Jubi- lee Committee came to the ground. How- ever, as works were stopped, as the air was purified, and as wages were paid, Widnes was jubilant after all.

It was a considerate and graceful thing on the part of Canon Eyre, of St. Helens, to in- vite the Rev. R. J. Ward, Congregational minister, to take part in the Jubilee Thanks- giving service at the Parish Church by reading the Lesson specially appointed. It was a practical acknowledgment of the fact that the Church is wider than the Establishment. The effect was altogether ood. " One touch of nature makes the whole (church) kin."

The following sentence is from the message of congratulation of the President of the United States to Queen Victoria :—" May liberty flourish throughout your empire, under just and equal la rs, and your Government be strong in the affections of all who live under it, and I pray God to have your Majesty in His holy keeping" It does not need much reading between the lines to perceive that this is intended to set her Majesty thinking about unhappy Ireland.

There is some fear that the new sixpences may be gilt and passed off as half sovereigns. "Guilty" will be the sentence passed upon any one caught in the act. It is stated that Lord Randolph Churchill considers that the half-sovereign is unpopular. He is mistaken; let him visit his constituents with about 10,000 of th.3m. He will find that he and the half-sovereign will be enthusiastically re- ceived.

The brutality of the constabulary at the Irish evictions seems to have been emulated by the policemen who have been engaged in the tithe war in Wales. It is all very well to say that the law must be enforced, but it is not quite clear that the best way of doing it is by breaking limbs and laying heads open. The massacre at Peterloo was, professedly, an enforcement of the law. The Tories when in office have usually a disorderly way of preserv- ing order.

The Bishop of Liverpool, in laying the. foundation stone of St. Mary's new school at Great Sankey. aptly described it as a jubilee School. And good jubilee work too. The Rev. E. S. Jackson has gone about the matter in the right spirit. He literally led the way with a subscription of Ezso. Mr. Jeans has behaved handsomely too in giving the freehold site. No wonder that, with such zeal, the Committee can see their way to £BOO out of the £1,300 required. '

The sufferers from foreign sugar bounties had a meeting in Liverpool the other day; and some strong language was used. We were promised that all these things should be made right when the Tories got in office. How is it that these men are still left crying in the wilderness ? Is it that Lord Salisbury is helpless, or indifferent? Or are we to un- derstand that it is another instance of the great margin between Tory promise and Tory performance ?

THE NEW COINAGE.—The Bank of England has commenced the issue of the new coinage, for which a very large number of applications have been re- ceived from London and provincial bankers. The amount of the issue is as yet indeterminate, and the Batik will go on supplying until the demand falls off. Applicants, however, do not receive all they ask for, but generally about one-third, as the amount coined so far is not very large, and' there is a large stock of old coins in hand fit the Mint. Coins of every denomination have been issued, including the double florin, for which there was a good de- mand, and the £5 piece. There is an idea that these latter coins are not intended for circulation. That is not so. Naturally, the number struck will be limited; but they will circulate quite as legally as any other coin of the realm, although no doubt mast of them will find their way to the cabinets of numismatists, or be otherwise kept as mementoes of the Jubilee year.

The ex,tra sale of the paper on Saturday will afford a special opportunity to advertisers. Newsagents are requested to order early. TRE LATE MR. CHORLTON OF RPNCORN.—As a mark of respect to the memory of the late Mr E A Cherlton, whose , death was recorded last week, the b-111 of the Parish Church on Sunday were muffled. Mr. Chorlton was a sidesman of the church. Prior to the morning service the Dead March in Saul " was played on the organ by Mr Johnson. The Rev A P Hol me, M A.. rec•or of Tattenhall, alluded to the sad event, and at the New Church of St Michael's and All Angels reference was also made by the Rev J H A Elatcheson, TIIE WIDNES WOUNDING CASE.— At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, John Mitchell, a respectably-dressed young many, who was employed as a clogger by Mr Hall. of Meraey road, was brought up on remand charged with haying, on the 16th Met, unlawfully wounded John McConeghy, a workman for Messrs Hutchinson and C , chemical manufacturers, by stabbing hint with a knife The circumstances have been published in this joi.rreal. and the Bench having heard the evidence and the stet-- rnent by Mr Knowtes for the defence, committed the prisoner to the Sessions for trial. Bail was refused. A JUBILEE Einar AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty See- sines, on Thursday, Ellen MeLannaghan' a married woman,, was charged with committing a breach of the peace. P.C. Holbrook stated that on the previous night there was a row in the street, and the defendant would not leave but con- ' tinned to excit- the people to disturbance. He seiz,cl hold of her, and after a struggle of ten minutes' diration, during which time his troueers were torn and his fact scratched, Are succeeded, with the Rid of several civilian, ire locking her no. The deferidaht called two witnesses, who said that Mrs McLanneglian never moved from her own doorway As the conetable watt passine along she remarked that the ' disturb ince that was going on was a Juhilee tight," where- upon thc constahle seized hold of her, dragged her along the street, :MA Mewed " upon her. The Bench consi- dered there was a doubt in the case, and dismissed the woman.

VISITORS TO BLACRPO.iL should alay at the Station Torn- ' perance Hotel, right opposite Central station. Central position. Commodious and accommodating. Terms easy —Apt,ly J. Heap.—.Ad ' JuBILED CELEBaATioN AT WESTON.—Tbe congregation of the Weeleyau Chapel, Weeton, together with Ice day and leunday 00l children, celebrated the Jubilee by forming a procession. Before leaving the school at 2 p in., every- one in the procession was presented with a modal. Wag- gonettes accompanied the procession. Ttl.3 following route was taken :—Weston.road, Ureenway-road, Norm an-road, and Heath-road. The cross was r.mchad at 3.30, where a large circle was formed. -Here the braes band, which had headed the procession, played National airs. The National Anthem was afterwards Sung. The junior scholars were first served with tea, about 147 partaking. Tbe elder scholars and parents were then served. In all, 554 had tea. An entirely free house was kept ; all who presented them- selves were welcome. In the evening, various sports took place in a large field kindly lent by W Banks, Esq, J.P. Mr Kirkham distributed the r:tizes that had been won. A large bonfire on the Over Hill finished the day's rejoicings. ROBBING WIDNES PAWNBROKERS.—At the Widnes Police Court, ou Monday, Catherine Bryson, a single woman, whose place of abode is in Lugsdsle, was charged with stealing a pair of trousers, value 4s 61, the property of Mr. Frederick Neil, Anne-stt,et. West. On Friday evening the prisoner was in the shop, and after her departure tbe trousers could not be found. It was afterwards ascertained that they had been pledged at Mrs. Jamieon's pawnshop.— The prisoner wee also charged with stealing a pair of blankets, value 12, from the shop of Mrs. Jamison's, pawnbroker, Anne-street, West. The blankets were last seen in the shop on Tuesday evening, the 14th lest., by Miss Liu& Jamison, and on Friday evening they were discovered at the shop of Mr. Neil, where the prieener had pawned them .• There was a third charge against the prisoner of stealing two pairs of trousers and a cost, and a vest value 33s 6d, the property of Mr. F. Neil, pawnbroker. The articles were uot missed until shown to the assistant, Mr. Dixon; on Saterdsv last by P.C. Thompson. The prisoner pleaded guilty to each charge, and was sentenced to six weeks' imprisonment. KNrirE Tnnowtwo sa RUNCORN—At Runcorn Police Court. on Thursdsy. before Captain Hazlehurst, a respect- able looking man named John Morris was charged with feloniously and maliciously wounding Thomas Kennedy with intent to do some grievous bodily harm. From the statement of Superintendent Hollingwortb it appeared that the prisoner is manager of a shop in Bridge-street, belong- ing to Mr. Johnson, wholesale grocer, of St. Helens, and Kennedy is a carter in the same employ. For Borne time the men had not been on good terms, and an altercation between them took place on Wednesday morning. The prisoner eeized a large carving knife used for cutting bacon, and threw it at Kennedy, who was struck by the weapon on the left side und..r the arm pit, and received a wound which bled freely. He was taken to Dr. McDougall's enrgery at once, and Superintendent Hollingworth ordered the arrest of Morris.—Dr. McDougall deposed that the wound was an inch and a ball to two inches in length, and ran under the skin in the diniction of this shoulder blades. Had [Le wound ' been an inch and a Pall deep it would have penetrated the lung and the heart, bat the blow had apparently been di- verted by coming in contact with a rib. He hop-ti and believed that the more Important organs underneath had not been penetrated. The man was not in a fit condition to appear that morning. The wound was In a very dangerous , part of the body, and In the interest of Kennedy as well as , tbe prisoner he had ordered Kennedy to rest until Monday. —On this evidence Superintendent Hollingworth applied , for a remand until Monday, which was granted. Bail was refused.

1 BRRACLIRS OF TRH VACCINATION ACTS AT RUNCORN.— At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, G. rotge Smart, Wharton, of Weston, was charged with neglec,ing to have his infant daughter, Rose Marv, traccinard accordinir to the Vaccination Act of IS67.—Mrs Wharton said the child wan vaccinated by Dr. Mangan, but not successfully. Since then she had had chicken pox and several other ailments, and had not been in a fit condition to be vaccinated.—Mr. Colsburn, the vaccination officer, said he registered the birth of the child on the sth June, 1886. On the 6th October he received a certificate of postponement of vaccination until November 7th. but since that day Mrs Wnarton had taken no steps to have the child vaccinated, and no answers had been given to the notices he had served.—Mrs Wharton said she was not against vaccination.—Mr. Brundrit remarked that her offenc-e was that she had neglected to provide the necessary certificates of postponements. They were bound to convict, and she would he fined 23 6d, and costs, 98 61. --William Faulkner, of Collier-street, was summoned on a charge of neglecting to have his son, Thomas Fleet Faulk- ner, born on the 30. h August, vaccinated.—The defendant said it was not his wish that the child should not be vac- cinated, but it was not in a fit condition to undergo the oneration. Only five weeks ago they took the child to Dr. Mangan, who said it might die if vaccinated. Thn papers had been riven to the doctor to fill up and returq o Mr Colebern.—Mr. Brundrit said it was his duty to see that the papers were returned to Mr. Coleburn.—A fine of 2., and costs, 9s 6d, was imposed. The defendant asked if he could not appeal, and Mr. Johnson replied in the negative. FLOWER SERYICE AT RYNCORN.—The annual flower aervice in connection with Bethesda Congregational Chapel was held in that edifice on Sunday evening last. The building was tastefully decorated wan fhwering plants kindly lent for the occision by Messrs Philip Speakman, T Booth, Thomas Kirkham, and W H Chadwick. Many members of the congregation also carried bouquets of flowers which were collected at the'close of the service, and on Monday were distributed to the homes of the sick in the town. The decor,tions were in charge of Messes W H Chadwfck, P Ainsworth, 8 Watson, J Woods, E Bolver, W Heatherington, S Abrams, and Miss Edith Littler, Miss Speakman, and Mrs Thomas. Hymns specially selected for the occasion were sung, under the leadership of Mr P Ainsworth, the organist being Mr H Handley. The title of the discourse of the pastor, the Rev J D Thomas, was 'Bible flowers, and the uses which we make of them," and in the course of his remarks he said that although there were in Palestine about 2,000 species of flowers, not more than seven or eight were referred to in the Scriptures directly or by name. The flower most freqlent!y referred to was the lily, next the rose (a species of autumn crocus), then the flower of the vine, the almond flower, and the flower of grass, which latter Mr Thomas considered was a general term for all flowers growing in pasture land. There was one flower called " Henna" which, although not men- tinned in the authorised version, found a place in the revised version. The two principal uses of flowers, as set , forth in the Bible were—first, as models for works of art in connection with the tabernacle and temple ; and secondly, to illustrate the premature overthrow of long cherished schernee, and the frailty of human nature an I the brevity of human life, and to illustrate return of min to divine favour. There was a good congregation at the interesting service., HALF HOLIDAY UFSOBT.—Persons desirous of enjoying day in th 3 midst of beautof il country should visit the village nf flruft which has become rather famous of late owing to the evraordinary horned ponies which are still to be seen in the locality. Mr Guest personally con.mcted the excursion, and a moat pleasant and instructive time was spent among.; the numerous ohkesta of interest. JUBILEE VERSE AT Ruscortw.—We understand that His Royal Highness the Ptrinc.. of Wales has been gra- dough, pleased to accept copies of poems composed Ist Mr D H Jones, draper, Runcorn, titled "A. Jubilee Plea,"j "Jubiles Ole," and "Moe/ Famtnau'a Tower." The Prince Of Wales has directed the Comptroller of the Household to acknowledge their receipt from the Rev S P Jones, Welsh We.levan Minister, Epworth Villa, Llanfairfechan, formerly of Widnes, who forwarded dual copies to enable His Royal Highness t send coulee to Her MHjsety the Queen, and to thank the Rev S P Jones for the same. SENIOns ASSAULT AT Drrrow.—Michaal C4TIPV. chemi- cal laboure,,J hnson st,Ditton,wassum at, ned toViiid• a ,Petty Sessions, as 1 hursday. to ansmer a charge of alseaulting Hannah Barnett, on tiv, 18di inst. It was alleged by the complainant, and bar statement was confirmed by several witnesses, that on the day named ehe was sitting on the doorstep of her dwelling, when the prisoner went up to her and felled her to the ground with a bg piece of wood which he carried in his band. She was rendered insensible, and lay in that condition for a considerable time. On the same evening, P.C. Hudson asked the prisoner why he had thus attacked the woman, and he replied that she bad been throwing at his dsor. Tne Bench imparted a fine of 20s and costs, or a month's hard labour. RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY . AUTHORITY.— A meeting of this body was held at the Workhouse, at Dutton, on Thursday, under the presidency of Col. Ashton. The following members were also present: The Revs. J. Lockwood and J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. T. Hadfield, J.. Parr, J. Brandreth, and E. Aaron, with the clerk (Mr. IL Linaker). deputy-clerk (Mr. W. H. Linaker), and inspector of nuisances (Mr. J. Farrington).--The Inspector of Nuisances reported that since thelast meeting of the Authority he had been busily engaged in inspecting a number of cow- sheds, &c., and that he intended to continue such inspection throughout the district. He also reported that certain farm premises, situate in Kingsley, were without a water supply, and - suggested that the attention of the agent be called to the matter. A nuisance existed on premises situate in the same township, and a pool at The Hurst was reported to be in a very foul and offensive condition. —The mem- bers discussed the matters referredto, and the Board gave the Inspector instructions to call the at- tention of the agent. of the four houses at Kingsley to the deficient supply of water, and alsh to acquaint the Medical Officer of Health with the nuisance in the same township, and request him to report thereon. The Inspector was order to call upon the owner of the pool situate at The Hurst, and ask him to abate the nuisance. THE EDUCATIONAL COXIMISSION. The Educa- tional Commission met ,on Thursday, and among others, took evidence from Mr. Twits, master of the British School, Warrington. and Mr. BodingtOno principal of the Yorkshire College, Leeds. •, , SWTHE FEVER .A.ND RABIES IN .CHESHIRE.—CoI.. Hamersley, Chief Constable of Cheshire, has received notification of 39 outbreaks of swine fever on eight fresh farms in the townships of Brereton, BaddeleY,• Dunham, Eaton, Haslington, Wallasey, Weaver- ham, and Great Warford. 'There are also two cases of rabies reported at Ashton-on-Hersey and Partington. INQUEST AT BUDWORTIL-011 Thursday evening Mr. H. B. White, Warrington, deputy coroner, held an inquest at the George and Dragon Inn, Great Budworth, on view of the body of Willian Mellor (71),a painters' labourer, in 'the employ of Messrs. Verdin. Evidence was given by Dr. Willett to the effect that on the 13th inst. he was passing Messrs. Verdin's works at Ashton, when he was called to the deceased, whose right hand and arm had been severely crushed, and who was also suffering from. severe shock to the system. Witness prescribed for him, and sent him, home, but it was afterwards' found necessary to amputate -.part • of the arm. Rapid prostration subsequently tat in, and deceased died last Tuesday. Further evidence was given, to the effect that when at work deceased accidentally had his hand crushed between the buffers, of two railway waggons. The jury returned a verdict to the effect that the deceased died from prostration, following injuries,accinentally received , TAKING A HOWIE AND CART: "A MAD FREAK." —At the St. Helens Town Hall, on Saturday, Jas. Geogaghan, of Margaret-street, Widnes, was charged with stealing a horse and cart and a quantitylof groceries, together of the value of about £B5, the property of Margaret Hampton, of Almond-street, Parr.' The 'prisdner was remanded for a week.—On Monday two young Men named Thomas Edward Jackson, of 19, Davies-street, Widnes, and Hugh Hughes, of 35, Hartley-street, Widnes, were charged with being concerned in the same robbery. It ap- peared that on. Friday night the prosecutrix, who is a carrier at Parr, was 'returning from Warrington with a cart load of groceries, &c. She stopped at the Tipping's Arms public-house, at Bold, and when she came out she found that the horse and cart, and the contents of the latter, had gone. The prisoners were seen to drive off with the horse and trap and they were followed and captured. On being charged with the offence, the prisoners said they did not intend to steal the things. Jackson in- formed. the Bench that it was only. done in a mad freak while all the three of them were drunk. The prisoners were remanded until Friday, and were admitted to bail, themselves in £lO and two sure- ties of .£5 each.

RUNCORN HILL QUARttlES.—Guest and on v. Brun- drit and ('o.—Yesterday week, before Mr. Justice Kay, in the Royal Courts of Justice, an application for an injunction was made by Mr. Marten, Q.C. (in- structed' by Messrs Grundy, Kershaw, and Co., as agents for Messrs. Linaker and Linaker, of Riinciorn, solicitors for the plaintiffs), to restrain the defend- ants, Messrs. Brundrit and Co., their servants and agents, until the hearing of the action, or furthe; order, from representing themselves to be the pro- prietors of the Runcorn Hill Quarries, and from selling or offering for sale, or exhibiting or dis- tributing, or parting with any stone not brought from the Runcorn Hill Quarries as stone from the Runcorn Hill Quarries. Mr. Henderson, who ap- peared for the defendants (on the instructions of Messrs. Cole and Jackson, as agents for Messrs. It. Davies and Co., of Warrington, defendants' solici- tors), submitted to a perpetual injunction with costs in the terms asked, and also to an inqui7 as to damages. The Runcorn Hill stone is well known throughout the country as a hard, durable red sandstone, and• it was alleged that the defendants have for some time on their letter paper. and by means of cards, been advertising themselves as the proprietors of the above quarries, although as a matter of fact they have no quarry in Runcorn Hill, the plaintiffs being the sole lessees thereof. NEWTON • RACES: INTERTNTING COMMENTS.— Speaking of Newton races, last week, a sporting contemporary observes; "If shorn of the import- ance which once characterised the Cup Day at New- ton, we nevertheless welcome it as an old friend; and we, who can remember witnessing the Newton Cup for nearly five and twenty years, could associ- ate a world of Turf history with its decision that would read like a fairy tale to those who only know Lancashire racing in recent years. Who is there that can remember the opening of the Newton branch line from the main line, near Earlestown Jpnction, to the course. Who cannot recount the breakdown of the. engine, and the clambering up clay embankments, until the broadcloth then ob. tamable for suits was a compound of black-cloth and yellow-coloured mud. Ten, eleven, and twelve o'clock struck, and still the unlucky voyageurs had not returned to Manchester. The writer once re- members his sire and a relative turning up in the early hours of the morning, in a state of mud and bewilderment not easily described. The branch line is now unused. It was condemned as unsafe some few years back, and now the direct way is either to Newton Bridge or to Earlestown Junction. The remainder of the distance must be eithernegotiated on shank's pony or by trap. In the days when the branch line was first used the county families drove to the Newton course in four-horsed coaches. They were the natural stands that were then in general use; and the erection of the Newton Grand Stand—one of the most commodious and best in the Kingdom—was quite an event in the district, whilst the hot dinners in its saloon were one of the proverbial features in a visit to Newton, for, no matter the heat, your, true-bred Lancastrian can always feed. Quicker communication has changed the pidnie character of the earlier Newton meetings to a purely business gathering, and the present generation of racing men have no more idea of the jolly meeting the Willow S furnished our fathers than they have of the pre-historic period, which is a cut above the imagination of those who have not a soul above the hacknbyed 'Six to four on the field,' which is so constantly dinned into our ears now-a-' days."

div.p: should be given _them to better their condi-
tion—to enable them to step out of the mire into which through no fault of their own they,
unhappily._ find -themselves.
England has
done her duty in part by providing hospitals . _ . .
• for the diseased _in body and mind; but it
cannot be said of her that she has done it
wholly until by her statesmanship, and by the application of her vast material resonrces, the way shall be made easy for those who are born
in the gutter to crawl out of .it, in the lively

hope Of becoming contented and reputable citizens. The bitter cry has oeen raised, and will not cease until a change is effected either by reform or revolution. We must not de- spair; progress is the law of beinz, and so much has been done since Queen VICTORIA
ascended the throne that we may well hope
I or better thinas in the future.

THERE is to be "a great national party," and Mr. CHAMBERLAIN and Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL are to be its prophets and its pillars. They have made friends and em- braced each other as brothers, and hence- forth England is to be a happy land. There may be people who have their doubts as' to , whether oil and water can be made, to mix in this way; but the leaders of the new depar- ture have none; they have only to come together and the nation will be transformed. Caw me, caw thee for six months has been hatching, This scene of Joseph's itch and Randolph's scratching. We can quite understand why Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL should humour Mr. CHAMBER- LAIN in this fanciful idea of "a national party ; " he knows perfectly well that it will be the Tory party with another name. He is angling for big fish, and he will use any sort of bait that will serve his purpose. His lord- ship is just now out in the cold with his party; but he is aiming at setting Lord SALISBURY aside, just as Mr. CHAMBERLAIN aims at supplanting Mr. GLADSTONE. It may seem very ludicrous to onlookers, but the principals are very serious on the matter. They have great faith in themselves -; aid there is no doubt that they are capable of doing great things apart from each other; but put them in harness together and they will soon pull each other to pieces by pulling different ways. To begin with, they are not even in agreement on the Irish question. Lord RANDOLPH. in his speech at Trowbridge on Saturday evening, made a dead set at Home Rule, and suggested that they were knocking the bottom out of it. But Mr CHAMBERLAIN is a Home Ruler. He has said again and again that he was in favour of the principle of Home Rule, although on posed to the Home Rule Bill. How has this little difference to be settled? Has Mr. CHAMBERLAIN to cease to be a Home Ruler. or has Lord Randolph to become one? This is a point that will have to be determined be- fore the "great national party" can be formed. Followers will require to know I whither they are being led, unless they are, to quote one of his lordship's polite phrases, "hopeless idiots." "Popular sympathy" is all very well as a text to preach on; but the test question is—what does it mean? The member for Sow h Oaddington points to the Allotments Bill in the House of Lords as evidence of the wAy the Tories are coming round to Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S views. Well— If it be so, why it is so, you know; And if it be so, so be it.

But we are a trifle sceptical as to this sudden conversion to the .doctrine of "Three acres and a cow." The fact is the Tory party have not yet ceased to deride it and they must in- deed be "hopeless idiots" to mock themselves in this fashion. And, then, what about Free Education, and Disestablishment ? Are these to be planks in the new platform? Or is Mr. CHAMBERLAIN going to efface himself by be- coming a little brother of Rip Van Winkle? And what about the Skeleton of the Feast. and Lord SALISBURY? Is it to be supposed that they will look quietly on whilst the ill- matched pair set about knocking the bottom out of the tub upon which they stand? Bab I "a great national parly," with two such leaders as the member for West Birmingham and the member for South Paddington, is an ugly conception born of a disordered brain : it is a "Vision of Sin." And yet let us be frank enough to admit that Mr. CHAMBER- LAIN and Lord RANNOLPH CHURCHILL are at one point in accord; they agree in hatina Mr. GLA DSTONE But hatred is poor material to work with ; it may serve to form another Cave of Adullam ; butit will not do as the fc,un- dation of "a great national party.

_aly, the proprietor of the Pomona, is almost in ruins. The roof was burst in, the windows smashed, and chairs and property were broken to an enormous extent. In Ordsall-lane, near Messrs. Haworth's mill, a great amount of damage was done. The windows and fronts of shops and houses were blown down, and some people were hurt. In a small cottage / near the works a second fatalitytook place. Th e house was wrecked, and a, little girl, the child of a man named Heald was so injured that death resulted late in the day. The child had been sickly, and lay , in its cradle. When the explosion occurre I, the cradle was lifted bodily from its position and dashed against the wall. The Manchester fire bri- gade had a hard task in subduing the different fires but the nearness of the canal gave them • an excell- ent supply of water. There was some danger at the time of further explosions, and efforts were speci- ally directed to avoid such a calamity. In this risky work the men behaved admirably and with success.

The Clerk read a petition which had been for- warded to the Board for •signature against the opening of public-houses on Sundays. The peti- tion pointed out that the sale of intoxicating drinks was the cause of domestic misery, pauperism, and crime, and, therefore, the petitioners desired to see public-houses closed all day on Sundays except to the bona fide traveller.—On the. motion of the Rev. J. Lockwood, seconded by Mr, Fisher, it was deci- ded that the petition should be placed on the table.

_ TIM BOARD AND DR. MACDOUGALL. The Clerk read a letter he had received from Dr: Macdougall; of Runcorn, dated 20th June, 1887, Acknowledging the receipt of letter forwarded by the Clerk on the Bth instant, in which Dr. Mac- Dougall was asked to explain, for the information of the Board, why Elizabeth Howcroft, the wife of Robert Howcroft, of Weston, received a recommend for one pint of brandy and six pounds of beef. The Medical Officer replied that Robert Howcroft was blind, and unable to do much more for himself than eat the food which was provided for him, and sit by the fireside from morning until night. His wife had been suffering from cancer of a very exhausting character, and he ehought it his duty to give her the recommend, as she lived a considerable distance from the nearest licensed house, where she could be supplied with brandy in case of emergency. Directions were given for her to be supplied with beef, to be made into tea and he did not think that a pound of beef, maCle into a pint of tea, and consumed in 2/1 hours, was exces- sive under the circumstances, neither did he think that the brandy, even if the whole of it were con- sumed in the time named, would be too large a quantity in such a case. The Clerk thought that Dr. McDougall might have given the Board that information when the first letter was written, and thus saved the time of the Board.— Mr. Wallington moved that a letter be written to , the effect that Dr. McDougall be requested to give a straightforward answer to a straightforward question.—The Rev. J. Lockwood thought that the reply given now would be sufficjent for the pur- poses of the Board. He thought, however, that Dr. MacDougall should be requested to give a direct answer, and not equivocate as he had done.—The motion was seconded. —On the resolution being sub- mitted to the meeting, it was carried by six to I , four

ST. MICHAEL'S ANI) ALL ANGEL'S CHURCH, RUNCORN OPENING CEREMONY.

IThe Church of sr. Michael and Al! Angel's, Greenway- t road, Was opened for public worship on Sunday. The edi- fice has been erected to meet requirements of the district of Newtown, a part of the town which has rapidly developed. On the plans the building is shown with a tower and epire, and a chencel and transepts, lat.t owing to a lack of funds only the nave has at present been erected. The construc- tion at the porting mentioned has been indefinitely post- poned. As at present arranged, IF)rvi ver, the bui.diog is well fitted for divine service. The nave is 86 feet by 27 feet, with north and south aisles, each 77 feet by 13 feet; and entrance is effected by porches placed at the south- west corner and the north-east side of the building, there being double doors for the prevention of draught.. The church is the early decorated style of Gothic architecture, I with traceried and mullioned windows in the aisles and I clerestary and east and west ends of the church. The !whole of the walls of the building erect Runcorn red sand- ; wone faced with the same tone in regular courses. The ; wood work is of the beet selected pitch pine verniotbsd. The principal trusses of the roof h +ye circular luminat+ d ribs (moulded) with carved bones at the intersections, and the feet of all, the principals are supported on carved red sandstone corbels The floors are formed of wood blocks, kid in herring bone patterns on concrete, and is as nearly 'al• possible noiseless. The roof is covered with West- mo-eland green elates, and the ornamental ridges are of , red terra' netts. The glazing is of rolled cathedral glass ,in geometric lead patterns. Messrs J D Barry & Sons, of Liverpool, were the architects, and. Mr Richard Birkett, of Hartford, was the builder. Mr H. Coward was the , clerk of works. There is comiderable ground round the Ichurch, which is enclosed by a wall and high iron rail- ; !Rocs erected by Messrs T. Kirkham d: Co ,and while now ; the building presents a by na means unplessing appearance, when the chancel and boxer and spire are added, the ! effect will be greatly ent arced. he opening services ' I were conducted on Tuesd.y last. In the morning the prayers were read by the Vicar (Rev A Maitland Wood), 1 and the Rev J. H. Acheson, of St. Peter's, Cheater, read the Lesson, and preached a sermon from the 27th verse of the lot chapter of Philliplaus. He observed that the , Church was an indication of growing life, but it WAS not' Intended that the chancel arch should remain blocked up as it was that day, but that the work should be perfected very speeitily. In the evening the Rev A. P. Helms, MA., of Tattenhall, preached to a good congregation. The services were full choral. Services in conn.clon with the same event were also held at the Parish Church, Mr Holme oc- cupying the pulpit in the morning and Mr Acheson in the evening. Collections were made in aid of the funds of thei new church. •

ANOTHER MAID KING OF BkVARIA. - King Otto or Bavaria is now olficielly declared to be incurably insane. It is not surprising, therefore. that It is again rumoured that the Prince R-gent may shortly ascend the throne as King, the unfortunate Otto being formally deposed. RESULT OF THE SHIP CANAL INQUIRY. At the meeting of the Select Committee on Fri- day morning, 'Mr. Childers intimated to counsel that the committee were not going to review the finan- cial estimates of 1885 except so far as they might. be affected with the present bill, and they would be glad if the learned gentlemen would take note of the fact. They also desired Mr. Pember to limit himself to replying on Mr. Bidder's statement as to the insufficiency of capital. Mr. Pember then went on to controvert the figures put forward by Mr. Bidder on Thursday, and asked if they got their £7,000,000 how could the state of things put for- ward by their opponents interfere with the provi- sions of the clause 38. The room was then cleared, the public being re-admitted in about five minutes. The Chairman said they found the preamble proved,. but they would require in sub-section 4 of clause 2 that not only shall the whole of the ordinary shares. be allotted, but that £2 per share shall have been paid. There were also two probable amendments about which they would not say anything at pre- sent. One was that in clause 4 the words no prefer- ence shares shall be issued ought to be " allott ed." The committee also doubted whether it might not be necessary in consequence of their requirements about the payment of £2 per share, there should not be some slight extension of time. Under the Act as it stood, the seventh or eigl4h of August was the , date fixed, and they would hear counsel on this point whether some slight extension might not be neces- saiT.v-Mr. Brown said with regard to the first two points there was no difficulty, but there was with regard to the extension of time.—The Committee then adjourned for half an hour, and when it rear, sembled, counsel for the opponents had retired, and the agents announced that further opposition was reserved for the House of Lords.—lt was ultimately decided that the clause should run that £6 of pre-. ference capital should be called for each £2 of ordinary, so as to establish an equilibrium between. the Lancashire and the capitalist money.—Mr. Pember intimated that the promoters did not wish to proceed with the question ot the extension of time owing to the great technical difficulties in the way.

A SINGLE STONE

from a running brook s?ew tfie giant Goliath, and many noble man since that time has died from a single stone in the kidney, which might have been dissolved and carried away had the proper means been used. Mr. George Wood- head, of 23, Burleigh-street, Holderness-road, Hall, was aware 1.1 this fact, as the following statement shows:— tie says :-- About three years ago I began to pass blood with my water, which gradually increased in quantity, and was accompanied by a frequent and irritating desire to urinate with great straining The doctor I consulted was unable to help me with his medicine, and I grew worse, until I finally became so seriously ill that I was obliged to take to my bed. I employed the best medical talent in Hull, and was treated for a long time, kut without benefit. The doctors finally told me that my trouble was undoubtedly due to atone in the kidney, and I would have to go to the hospital and have it cut out, as there was no other cure. Being well advanced ha years, it was only a chance that I could survive the shock of so serious an operation, :pal did not go, much preferring to die a natural death. I became so prostrated that my pulse could not be felt at the wrist, ' and I made all arrangements, so far as possible, for my death, even selecting pall-bearers. - , The Lord Chancellor took his seat at 420 p.m. SMOKE NUISANCE ABATEMENT (METROPOLIS) BILL.-.-011 the motion to go into Committee on this Bill, moved by Lord SrasTICEDEX and CAMPBELL, Earl BROWNLOW moved .the rejection of the measure, stating that the machinery toy means of which the noble lord proposed to accomplish .the abatement of the smoke nuisance in the metropolis was not such as could in any way commend itself to her Majsty's Government—Viscount CRANBROOK re- marked that the opposition of the Home Office arose 'from the fact that in their opinion the machinery pro- vided by the bill would inevitably fail. In view, how- ever, of the strong opinion expressed in favour of the further consideration of the measure the Government had no objection to its reference to a select committee. —lt was referred accordinelv. p THE LAND TRANSFER BILL.—The LORD CHANCELLOR, in moving to go into Committee (on recommitment) upon this hill, said he had considered the various sugges- tions which had been made in the course of the progress of the measure, and had endeavoured as far as possible, to meet them.—Lord Flerschell entertained some 'doubt as to whether the scope and purpose of this bill were thoroughly understood. An impression prevailed that its provisions were more drastic and far-reaching than would prove to be the case. If the public believed :that It would produce any very speedy result, or that it vas a great step in the direction of a rapid realisation of la system of complete registration of the land of this country, they were likely to find themselves disan- pointed.—The House then went into committee on the. bill.—Ten clauses we'll agreed to, and progress was reported. ; Their lordships adjourned at 7 20 p.m. until Thursday. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—Mornes.

„ • The Speaker took the chair at 4 p.m. FORGED PETITIONS. Sir C. Fotesree stated that the Committee on Public Petitions had, after much inquiry, come to the conclu- sion that there had been an organised system of for, gerien with respect to petitions relating to the con- tinuance of the cod and wine dues. Though reluctant ,tlestrike the mitthr criminal, yet the ease against Bid- mend was cleat, end he moved, "That Reginald Bid mead, having fabricated signatures to certain petitions pre- sented to this House, ha l been guilty of a breaeh of the privileges of this House." Mr. BeenhAneu did not intend to oppose the motion. Tip chairman of the Committee on Petitions naturally , eael he felt a reluctance to strike at the minor criminal , while the greater ones escaped. (Hear, hear.) He thoalCht the course he (Mr. Bradlaugh) had taken was fillip justified by the report of the Committee. He did net intend to throw the least slight upon the report of the Commitee ; but he intended to suggest that the Coy- potation of the City of Tienclon were the greater criminals—(Onposition ebeers)—and there was over- wheltnine evidence that the gross negligence referred to bos the Committee was that to which every active mem-, , her of the 'Corpre.:-.: 1:1 of the City of London had been party. Gross negligence in one case might be over- looked, but this had gone on for a series of years, in relation to the same matter and after deliberate warn. ring. He thought he was fully warranted in describing this Corporation as the greater criminals. (Cheers and ' "No.") He Appealed to the House not to send this poor ' tool Bidrnead to gaol, whilst those who had encouraged '-hiet during the last sew or eight years escaped. He vronld suggest thatßidmead be instructed to attend the Reuse on Thursday and be reprimanded, the object of the reprienand being to touch the crime. A reprimand at the I baPwould, be a reprimand to a class of criminals who degraded the political activity of the people. Sir 'R. N. Fowhen supported the motion of Sir C Forster. This man had betrayed the confidence reprised in him •by those who employed him. ("Oh," and lalghter.) He was employed to do a perfectly legitimate thing—to talE6 petition.; from house to house, and to a,* people if they were willing to sign it. He betrayed the ' c'enfidence of those who employed - him. (Renewed j Waghten) As regarded the observations of the hon. neember for Northampton, as he had given notice that at , %future day he would charge him (Sir R. N. Fowler) JTO perjury he would not answer his remarks. ("Oh.') j „Mr. W. Loiniert thought the Committee had come to , a-very proper conclusion. After further discussion the' original motion was agreed to. Sir C. FORSTER then moved that Reginald Bidmead do attend this House, on Thursday next, at four o'clock, to be reprimanded by Mr. Speaker. • This was also agreed to without a division. ' •411 the motion 'of Sir C. Foasrett the petitions com- plained of were ordered to be cancelled. • SUPPLY.

On the vote for £25,982 for the maintenance and repair of Royal Palaces, Mr. Brant-avon expressed, his intention to divide , against the vote in order to assert his opinion that the Government ought to present with the estimates a memorandum showing the total cost of the Royal family. , The committee divided, voting: For the reduction, 62; gainst-. 105; majority against; 43. COAL MINES REGULATION BILL.

Mr. Marra:Piers moved that the House go into com- mittee on this bill. Mr. Bunr remarked that the measure made no altera- tion in principle with respect to the employment of girls and women about the pit. The time had come when this relic of barbarism should be abolished. (Cheers.) Mr. STAVELEY HILL hoped the House would hesitate before they deprived women of that employment by which they were earning an honest and much-needed wage.—Mr. F. 8. POWELL supported the bill.—Mr. 'Fmrwrca regretted that the limit of the age of boys had not been raised. gr. TOMLINSON claimed that the recent deputation of pit women was entirely spontaneous. He thought the Government entitled to praise for introducing the bill. Mr. Atherley-Jones and Mr. Pickard criticised some or the provisions of the bill, which were defended by Mr. Stuart-Wortley. After discussion, the debate was adjourned. The House atjjourneditt_l.3s a.m. until ' .day. HOUSE OF COMMONB.—WEDNESDAY. Mssow ,moved an amendment to provide that boys between 12 and 16 years of age should not be employed in mines more than 48 hours per week. —Several hon. members opposed the amendment as one which would add to the difficulties of worki,pg collieries.— Mr. John Ellis moved to leave Cut "girls," with the object of checking the employment of girls and women. Mr. F. S. Powell, who opposed the proposal as one which would inflict great hardship, stated that the recent deputation to

the Home Secretary was suggested by the women them- selves, and did not emanate from the employers. The hon. gentleman was speaking at a quarter to six, wen, accord- ing to the rules of the House, the debate was adjourned. Mr. Smith announced that as he found many gentlemen were remaining in town with the sole object of watching the, progress of this bill, he proposed to take it as the first order next day —(Cheers.) i Tax Entrcan iow Acrs —Captain Heathcote brought n a bill to enable children to earn exemption from school fees by regularity of attendance, and to amend the Elementary Education Acts in other respects. The House adjourned at six o'clock. HOUSE OF LoRDS.—TarrasDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat at a quarter past four o'clock.

There was a short d'scussion on the naval volunteer movement on a motion by Earl Cowper for certain corres- pondence. After the Premier had promised that the dov- ernment would find the noble lord an opportunity for again raising the question of the relations of the naval volunteers and the Admiralty the motion was withdrawn. Their lordships adjourned at twenty minutes past five o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS, THURSDAY. _

The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. THE TITHE WAR IN WALES.—Mr. MATTHEWS Was ques- tioned respecting the conduct of the police at recent tithe collections in Wales, and in his reply he said that, while he saw no reason to depart from the opinion he expressed on Monday. be was willing to consider how best an impartial inquiry into the whole of the circumstances might be held. Mr. OSBORNE MORGAN said this decision of the right hon. geatleman would render it unnecessary for him to move the adj mrnment of the House in order to call attention to this matter.

The Earl of Derby is to be chairman, and amongst the other members are Mr. Alderman Harwood (Mayor of Manchester), and Mr. F. W. Maclean, M.P. NEW Cone.tax.—A number of questions were put about the new coinage.—The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER said the similarity between the sixpence and the half sovereign would bp reconsidered by the Mint Authorities. TECHNICAL EDUCATION.—Sr W. HART-DYKE informed Mr. F. S. Powell that he hoped on an early day to introduce a bill dealing with the subj Pct of technical education. FORGED PETITIONS.—Bidmead, the man who had ad- mitted fabricating signatures to petitions promoted by the Corporation of London, appeared at the bar of the House and was reprimanded by tbe Speaker. THE MINES BILL.—The House again went into Commit. the on the Mines Bill, and resumed consideration of the amendment prohibiting the employment of girls, which gave rise to a long discussion on the work of pit.brow , women —The amendment was defeated by 188 votes to 112. —An al: endment moved by Mr. Bum., that girls, women, and boys should not be permitted to move loaded pit tubs, trains, or skips, was rejected by 124 votes to 71.—Clause 8 was then added to the bill, and several other clauses were agreed to.—An amepdment by Mr. FENWICK previding for universal payment by weight was carried by 127 to 119.— Some other amendments were moved,but they were rejected, and Clause 13, as amended,was agreed to. Progress was then repored. and the House resumed. THE EAST INDIA AND CHINA MAIL CONTRACT.—The debate, adjourned from the 7th inst, on the Government motion for the approval of the East Ir,dia and China mail contract was resumed by Mr ANDERSON, who moved the following amendment :—" That this House disapproves of any contract subsi lieing any line of steamers to carry mails to the East for a long period of years without steps having been taken to assist the Canadian Pacific Railway, by a subsidy, to run a fast line of steamers from Vancouvetto Asia." The hon. member spoke at some length noon the commercial and military advantages of the Vancouver. Pacific route, which he said was less costly than the other. —The debate was continued till a late hour.

DRUNKEN/Ml—Elizabeth Wayne, a stranger, 'was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Irlam-street on Saturday night. P.C. Westhead proved the case. She was dismissed.—Jonathan Hilton, labourer, was charged with a like olVeze in Manchester-road, on Saturday night, and also with assaulting P.C. Bracewell. He was ordered to be kept in custody until 2 o'clock. ASSAM= ON THE POLlCE.—Alfred Walsh and Richard Neary, privates, were charged with being drunk and-dis- orderly in Horsemarket-street on Saturday night, and with assaulting P.C.'s Corcoran and Hennessey. Prisoners pleaded guilty to drunkenness, but denied the assault. They were each sentenced to one month's imprisonment,with bard labour. _ _ _
THURSDAY —Before Major Litton, Alderman Webster, and
Coilncillor 151att.

A DRUNKEN Pow.—James Kelley, Patrick Kelley, and Mary Mahoeey were charged with having been drunk and disorderly on the evening previous. Kelley was also charged with having assaulted P.S. Bowen, Mahoney with having assaulted P.C. Corcoran, and Mann ion with damag- ing the coat eta man named Oxley.—A row took place in a vaults, and the assistance of tbe police was secured. They ejected prisoners, who then committed the offences attriented to them.—The male prisoners were each fined 20a and costs, and the female prisoner was fined 10a, includ• ing cots. Durnsgmenss.—William Jackson, charged with having been dronk in Wilderspool-road, on the night previous, was ordered to pay is, the lock up fee.—A young man named Bothwell was fined 5s and costa for drunkenness. Are ABSENTEE.—Thomas Griffin, an absentee from the 4th 13attalion Liverpool Regiment, stationed at Altair, was remanded to the military authorities. FElDAY.—Before Dr. Gornall and Alderman Harrison.

_ a child of six years old, was summoned for committing damage to grass in *afield belonging to Mr. James Eairclough.—lt was explained that the case was brought simply as a deterrent, and the Bench. after admonishing the child, dismissed her. CHARGES or ASSAULT—Henry Beckett was summoned for assaulting James Oxley, on the 20th inst. Mr. A. Browne, who appeared for the complainant, said that both parties lived at the Twelve Houses, Howlev. and were in the employ of Messrs. Fairclough and Sons. On Monday night complainant was witnessing the dis- charge of fireworks, with his wife, when Oefen- dant came up and said something about his flower pots having been broken by complainantra children. Com- plainant replied that,be had no children, and that most probably defendant's own children had broken the pota. Defendant then knocked complainant's wife down,and struck comp'alnant on the face. in defence Beckett said that he got to high words with (be complainant, and that he re- ceived provocation. Ile was fined 20s and costs, £2 2i in. all.—Ellen Carr was summoned by Ann Leach for assault- ing her at Latchford on Monday. The case was dismissed.

The prisoner was also charged with travelling on the London and North-Western Rtilway from Liverpool tO Ditton without baying previously paid hi 3 fare. Night Inspector Eason, of Ditton Junction, erred that the prisoner arrived by the 11 p.m. train from Lime-street, and would neither produce his ticket nor pay his fare. He cursed very violently. The prisoner, who said he should have pot off at Edge Hill, was fined 10eand cora —Catherine Matthews for creating a disturbance in Lugsdale-road, on the nu tilt., was bound over to keep the peace for three months.

It is in these busy times a far cry back to Satur- day night. But the Lard Mayor's banquet to the representatives of literature, science, and art was too notable an event to; pass by without reference. It was Alderman Cotton, still unsuitably 'plain " Mr.," who, whilst Lord Mayor, introduced the fashion of specially recognising literature, science, and art at the Mansion House. , Up tolis time there had been the regulation banquets to her Majesty's ministers, judges, and so on. BLit for the rest the Lord Mayor's hospitality was reserved for aldermen and city magnates. Mr. Cotton, one of the most enlightened Lord Mayors of the generation, bad a strong leaning towards literature and the drama, and, whilst he was Lord Mayor, shocked his brother- aldermen and town.councillers by sumptuously en- tertaining poor players and literary "gents." The experiment was so successful that the example has been followed with more or less completeness by hi successors. Probably there never was a more sue- cessful gathering than that of Saturday. Everyone •syho is -anybody was there, from "Oh Mansion House hand" like Sala, down to Mr. Rider Haggard,. to whom the dinner was a novelty. The National Liberal Club weds nominally opened to its 6,000 members on Monday. But, as yet,, it is far from being in a state of completeness. The reading-room, dining-room, and smoke-room are pretty well forward; but the rest is chaos, dominated by workmen, There is, however, sufficient done to establish the fact that the National Liberals have come into possession of the finest dab house in the world. Tnerg is nothing like it in London, on the Continent, or. even in America, where they build palaces on the slightest provocation. It is not only that the new club house is commodious, convenient, and handsome, but its construction and decoration are strikingly original. Tiles in delicate shades of brown and primrose form a leading figure in the decoration, covering most of the walls and mak- ing it specially delightful in summer time. Of course the club, house, availing itself of all the latest resources of civilisation, is illuminated by the electric light, -very skilfully and tastefully utilised. The site itself, in addition to be- ing conveniently central, is exceptionally charming. ,In front of the broad tong terrace i 8 the greensward of the publie garden, then the broad highway of the " embankment, and next the river, with its bold curve from Blackfriars to Westminster Bridge. To the east lies the city, with St. Paul's standing grandly out in the misty atmosphere that broods over Lon- don. The club house will certainly take a first posi- tion amid the sights of London, and is a great pos- session for the National Liberal party. London society has always one ludicrous affecta- tion to the fore. Sometimes it is a phrase " doncha know," or a bend of the back, or—really pretty this —a little curtsey on meeting an acquaintance. The latest and perhaps the most ludicrous is the new way of shaking hands. I have always • been of the opinion that hand-shaking is essentially a non- sensical proceeding, though certainly it hasits uses. It is something to do whilst you can think of what to say on. meeting an indifferent acquaintance. It is essentially a European and, above all, an English custom, a matter of marvel at first sight to Eastern . peoples. But if we are to shake hands we may as

At the Old Ball Inn, Winwick-street, Warrington, on Wednesday afternoon, Mr. W. T. • Husband, deputy coroner, held an inquest regarding the death of John Thomas Cunnington, a fitter out of employ- ment, who had lodged some time" with a widow named McDonough, at 62, Johnzstreet, and who on Sunday morning was found dead in his bedroom, hanging to the bed post by a piece of cord that had , been wrapped round his throat.—Bridget McDon- ough, the widow with whom deceased had lodged, said, that he had been. living at her house for the last eight months. He was by trade a fitter, and she thought be would be about 50 years of age. He bad been out of work a long time, and lived on his club money. Latterly he had been drinking heavily. On Saturday last he came home at about five o'clock in the evening, and took off his shoes. . Remarking that he would have a lie down, he went upstairs, and witness saw no more of him until the following morning.— William Johnson, saddler, 2, Winwick-street, said that at about half-past six o'clock on Sunday morning, he was looking at the erection of Jubilee decorations in Winwick-street, when a young man nained Bryan McDonough came to him and said "A man has hung himself at our house." He went there and found deceased dead, and perfectly rigid. One of his feet was on the floor, and his knee was bent as though he had • bent down to tighten the cord that was round his neck.. Witness and a policeman cut the rope, which was tied round a nail at the top of the bedpost.—Bryan McDonough said that on Sunday morning he went to awaken the deceased, and found him hanging. Deceased had been drinking heavily of late. In answer to the Coroner as to why he did not cut the rope, witness said that "le wanted to keep out of the sight" of the deceased, as he. was very much frightened. The Coroner said that as far as could be gathered from the evidenca it appeared that the deceased had committed suicide, and that no one else had anything to do with his death. There was no evi- dence of insanity. —A Juror: I believe he committed suicide under temporary insanity.—The Coroner: If you think there is evidence of insanity you are entitled to say so, but it does not make much dif- ference now.—The Juror: I believe that no man in his right mind would do such a thing.—The Coroner: That is not whit the law believes, though. He has been drinking, and his mind might be unhinged by that.—Tbe jury, after a few moment's consideration, returned a verdict of feb de ae.

well clasp each other's paw and go through the pump-handle business in straightforward fashion. That is, however, a thing which would shock Lon- don society to-day. The proper way to shake hands is to raise the right elbow nearly as high as the chin, hold the fore-arm level and touch the band of the acquaintance who has gone through the same curious process. It is very ugly to look ! at—rather awkward to do. But it is the thing, and you will see it going ' on wherever society meets. Mr. Du Maurier has quietly taken notice of it, and in his exhibition now on view in Bond-street the performance isincidentally shown in two or three pictures. We are not likely again to have such a pageant as Tuesday's, but still there are some lessons to be learned from it, and I think one is theexcellent use that may be made of the Ambulance Corps. Imme- diately under my window, which was in Pall Mall, a station had been posted. There was the surgeon in his regimentals, and his assistant in uniform also, and about a dozen men with stretchers. From time to time a signal would be given, the bearers would go to the front and bring back their victim. A yard in St. James' Palace was converted into a surgery, and all the appliances were to hand. One poor fel- low who had fainted !straight off, dropping his rifle and falling back into the crowd, was found to have under his uniform two vests, two flannel shirts, and two others! His scarlet coat was so much too large for him that all this padding out was necessary. No wonder the poor fellow fainted. It is astonishing , how quickly all the decorations have' beenremoved. It seems to have taken but hours to clear away what it took days to put up. The rolls of red calico, the loyal mottos, and the Venetian masts will be carefully despatched, and like ornaments at a con- fectioner's supper, will do duty over and over again to the great profit of those who let them out.

THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL COMPANY.

A special meeting of shareholders in the Manches- ter Ship Canal Company was held on, Monday at noon, in St. James's Hall, Oxford-street, in order that their formal consent might be given to the bill of the Company now before Parliament? Sir Joseph C. Lee presided, and moved the following resolu- tion :—" That the consent of the shareholders of the Manchester Ship Canal Co. be, and the same is hereby, given to the promotion in the Present session of Parliament'of a bill entitled A bill to enable the Manchester Ship Canal Company to raise a portion of their capital by means of preference shares,' subject to such alterations , therein as the Directors may approve and. Parliament may. prescribe."—This was seconded by Mr. Charles Moseley, supported by Mr. D. Adamson and Mr. W. H. Houldiworth, M.P., and carried unanimously. The Directors of the Ship Canal Company have issued the following circular to those applicants for shares who have not sent in their letters of confirm- ation;—" Deansgate, Manchester, 21st June, 1887. —Sir,--I am requested to urge upon you most strongly 'the extreme importance, if you. have not already done so, of your at once Signing and return- ing your letter of confirmation. It may be interest- ing to you to know that in addition to shares allotted signed confirmations representing upwards of '.£2,000,000 of ordinary share capital have been received, whilst the number of dissents received is 4extremely small, representing an inappreciable amount of share capital. The share capital already allotted amounts to upwards of £750,000, and the shareholders at their meeting to-day unanimously confirmed the Course proposed. —I am, &c., A. H. Wintwonnr, Secretary." At a meeting of the Gorton Local Committee, Mr. J. Buckley, in the chair, it was unanimously re- solved, on the motion of Mr. T. B. Cooper, seconded by Mr., J. H. Jackson, That this meeting heartily approves of the action of the directors in proposing, to issue half their capital in preference shares, be- lieving the ordinary shares will be greatly bene- fited thereby, and urges all applicants for shares to return at once the forms sent to them for their assent." ' The directors of .the Manchester Ship Canal Com- pany exhibited several plans of their undertaking in the Merchant Company's Hall, Edinburgh, on Wed- nesday, and Mr. Marshall Stevens, manager, ex- plained their details to the large company of leading business Men of the city .assembled. Mr. R. A. Macfie, of , Dregborn, who presided, spoke of the scbeme as one of the most important that had ever been approached. Ire himself had long advocateda ship canal between the Forth and Clyde, and he be- lieved that if the Manchester Canal were suc- cessfully started there would soon be another in Scotland. , Pitocuunreas 'TN COMMITTEE. , On Thursday morning a Select Committee of the House of Commons, presided over by Mr. Childers, had under considerationthe Ship Canal Bill, which 4 'provides for the raising of £4,000,000 of preference capital. Lord Egerton, Sir Joseph Lee, and other directors of the company were present, as well as Sir Joseph Pease, M. 1),, Mr. C. N. Parker, &c. The promoters were 'represented by Mn Pember, Q.C., and Mr. Balfour 'Browne, Q.C. and the oppo- nents, who are the Mersey Dock Beard, the Liver- pool Corporation' and the London and North- Western Railway Company, by Mr. Pope, Q.C., Mr. Bidder, Q.C., Mr. Little, Q.C., Mr. Moon, and Mr. Squarey. The room' having been clesrpd and the public re-admitted, the Chairman inti- mated that inasmuch as the time Of the Committee was limited, and they were ,bound to report on Monday, lie trusted counsel on both sides would • confine themselves to the points before them and not travel beyond.—Mr. Pember,Q.C., in opening the case, said the object of the Bill was an extremely simple one, and would be gathered from the preamble, with whidi he pro- ceeded to deal in 'detail. The result, if this legisla- tion was passed, would be that half the share capital would be preference, and half ordinary; and, as a matter of fact, taking the statistics of the railway companies throughout the kingdom as a guide, he found that this was pretty much the case'all over the kingdom. Perhaps the preponderance was slightly in favour cif the ordinary shares;but it was so slight that it did not interfere with the main statement. The question of how the rpromoters were to raise theirmoney was an absolutely domestic matter upon the settlement of which no oone ought Ito be heard but themselves. Reading the three petitions presented against this 'Bill, he could not for the life of him see how this matter could be anything more than domestic to the shareholders of the Manchester Ship Canal.— Mr. George Whitworth; secretary of the 'Ship Canal Company, was called, and gave evidence las to the assent of the ordinary shareholders to the proposal contained in the present bill.—Sir Joseph Lee. de- puty-chairman of the company, was next4examined by Mr. Pember. He gave evidence regarding the previous history of the company. and as to the last arrangement entered into with Messrs. Roths- child.— In cross-examination by Mr. Pope, Sir Joseph Lee said Messrs. Rothschild and Boring were to get 4 per cent on the issue. The company would receive four millions of money, less .C 60,000. In reply to further questions, Sir Joseph lee said Mr. B. A, Walker had now taken the contract on the same terms as entered into with Messrs.
