In replying, Mr Speakman said there was an old saying. that nothing succeeded like success, and he was amply ree paid for any trouble he had had with the kno, leige that their celebrations had passed off so well, and that everybody • was eatiefied. (Appiause.) ..The audience then sang For he is a jolly good fellow" very heartily, and the band having played "Auld Lang Sync," the proceedings terminated. SERVICE AT THE PARISH CHURCH. An interesting service in celebration of the Queen's Jubi- lee was held at Runcorn Parish Church. on Monday even- ing. The sacred edifice was well filled by a devout congre- gation. Music formed a coneiderable share of the proceed- ings, the following choirs takieg part :—Parish Church. Newtown MiKiioll, Holy Trinity, and Weston, and the choir of St. Paul's Wesleyan Chapel. The hymn ‘`. 0 God our help in ages past" was sung as the precessional, and the introductory sentences were taken from music by Tanis. The "To Deem " was sung to McCartney' setting in P. The special psalm was rendered in music specially com- posed by the organist and condactr.r, Mr. J. J Mawr. The lesson,which was selected f. ern St. Peter ii, OIL was read by the Rev. W. Preston, MA., vicar of Holy Trinity, after which Handels coronation anthem " Xadok the Priest," was performed. .The suffrages were intoned by the Rey. J. D. Ozanne, 8.A., and the prayers were read by the Rey. G E. Tindall, B.A. The Rev. A. Maitland Wood, M.A., vicar, occupied the pulpit, and took for his teat Psalms xxii, 5 Ira the comae of his sermon the vicar said for such a one as Queen Victoria to have worn the crown of England for 50 years, we might well thank God. Let them imagine what woald have been the condition of thing 3 in this' country if, 50 years ago, instead of that delicate, and apparently hApiess, girl being placed on the throne, ar profligate prince had been crowned; or suppose there had been a headstrong and violent prmcl epee the throne, or that during the course of 50 years the crown had passed from one to another rapidly ; was it not likely tent in that period, which Mid been a period of ear- tension of human thought, a period during which they had become more self-willed--was it not likely that there would have been rebellion? Instead of haying bad 50 years of peacefnl and happy progress, it might have been that the onuntry had been driven into disunion. If they only looked at the increase in scientific knowledge, and in the knowledge of philosophy; if they only looked at the means of communication which bound the hearts of men more closely together not only in this land, but throughout the world ; if they considered bow art, poetry, prin log, musiO, and general culture had grown auct increased during the past fifty years; they must admit that God had blessed the Queen's reign. Let them therefore pray that her Majesty might be comforted with strength from God, and that when she passed away from this life she might be saved through, the infinite mercy of the Lord Jesus Chris, and wina-betrer crown—a crown of eternal life.—Before dispersing the. congregation joined heartily in the singing et the National Anthem.

The father

of this gentleman, who is now living with hi;, is 85 years of age, being the oldest minister in the Wesleyan connec- tion. Ile is now an invalid, having been confined to his home during the last few years. During his itineracy he laboured seven years in the West Indies. The scholars proceeded to the park, which was placed at their disposal through the kindness of sir R Brook, Bart. Games were freely indulged in until four o'clock. when a precession was again formed, and the children west to their respective schools to tea. All the teachers and. scholars of the parish
having been presenied with a medal were ail admitted to a free tea. While all the householders and their wives were

admitted by ticket, the whole of the expense of tea and sports was born by the fund subscribed by the parishioners. After tea sports of a varied character were resumed for the remainder of the day, the brass band being in attenclancs. To conclude the day's amusements there eras a beacon of large dimensi ms to be lighted at ten o'clock on the Cagle Hill. The hill is of a commanding height, and the fire could be seen for many miles round, and added another irk in the chain of signal fires throughout the kingdom.

THE ILLUMINATIONS.. As a fitting conclusion to the joyous occasion tbe com- mittee resolved upon a display of fireworks and a bonfire, and baying had a rest from the heat and turmoil of the day's proceedings, at dusk peo;ale were to be seen flocking in their hundreds to the common, where the illuminations bad to take place. The arrangements had been placed in charge of Dr McDougall, Messrs J R Frith, S Taylor, J Davies, and T Handley. and punctually at 9 30 the doctor set fire to the immense pile of wood that had been collected. IToder the superintendence of Mr Davies no less than 16, tens of wood had been amassed together in a heap 16 feet high, and baying a diame'er of 20 f,eet. The timber had been gives by Messrs Brundrit and Co, Messra Hazlehurst and Sons, Runcorn So ip and Alkali Co, Mr Phiiip Speakman, and Mr S T4ylor. and had been conveyed to the appointed place by Mr John Moore, carter, and the Runcorn Soap and Alkali Company. Over the methodically•arranged beacon." tar and paraffin oil had heenlooured, and immediately the light was applied, the inflammable pile sent up a flame which. quickly increasing in intensity and power, must have been visible a distance of many miles. A livid glare lighted up nearly the whole of the epansive common, and the thou- sands of people who had asaembled appeared so many nu- , couth goblins as the darkness became more dense. At ten I o'clock the pyrotechnic display commenced, and the scene was then one of weird gran leur. As the rockets whirred

FESTIVITIES AT DUTTON WORKDOUSE. At the Dutton Workhouse Jubilee Day was observ.d in a manner which was most satisfactory. The inmates, in ac- cordance with instructions received from the Guardians. were provided with a substantial dinner and tea, and the regutations fpr the discipline of the House were relax-d to allow the inmates more freedom. The building was appro- priately decorated. At one o'clock on Tuesday the ininees , assembled in the hall, and after singing the-National an. them partook of roast beef and mutton, and fruit pies. A gross of Jubilee medals nad been kindly sent for the inmates by Mr S Taylor, of Runcorn, each of whom, with a few exceptions, displayed them. In the Afternoon the old women were provided with an excellent cup of tea, and the children indulged in a variety of sports. A sack of nuts were sent by Ilds*Kirkham, of Runcorn, and that gee- tleman's kindness was greatly appret!lated. At six. o'clock in the evening a substantial tea WU partaken of by the in- mates, the meal being composed of thin bread and butter, cold beef, and ham. The children were also provided with buns. After the tables had been cleared an entertainment was given by the inmates, and votes of thanks were unani- mously proposed to the Guardians and others who had pro- vided the good things fer them, and the proceedings were brought to a close in a most suitable manner.

through the air and broke into myriad coloured globes, and the numerous other artistic compounds of gunpowder hissed and exploded, the children present, and there were many hundreds, screamed with delight, and the children of older grow h could not suppress their admiritton. The contract for the fireworks had been given to Messrs Ait- ken and Company, of Liverpool, and a man from that firm superintended their discharge. At one time it was intended that the beacon fire should send forth its light from the rock on Runcorn Hill, whence many a signal in days long since passed has flashed a mes- sage to the surrounding country, but the committee aban- doned the idea in consequence of the danger, the beacon I'OCFC and its approaches tieing on the edge of a deep and dangerous quarry. At the request of Mr Shaw, the mission- ary, however, Mr Guest had the precipitous rock guarded hy a strong fence, and the former energetic gentleman had a beacon sending forth a light that could be observed for many miles both in Cheshire and Lancashire. Mr Shaw also organised a torchlight procession. About eleven o'cleck 200 persons, each bearing a lighted torch prepared by Mr George Holland, commenced to walk in procession from the Hill, and, passing across the common, acted as guides to the people there assembled. As the cavalcade wended its way to the • town, the effect of the flickering lights was pleasing in the extreme. Upon arriving in the centre of the town the people gave three hearty cheers for the Queen, and then dispersed to their homes. Thus ended - a day that will be remembered by the old as long as life shall last, and by the young long after the noble lady in I whose honour the demonstrations were held shall have shuttled off this mortal coil. The harmonious and happy manner in which the entire day's proceedings passed off must have been highly gratify- ing to all concerned, and the Jubilee Committee, the mem- bers of which are too numerous to be mentioned, and the police, under Superintendent Hollingsworth, are alike to be congratulated on the termination of a busy and exciting day. It is worthy of remark that there was very little drunkenoese to be observed in the town. THE TREAT TO THE AGED POOR.

In the midst of all this jubilation, the poor and needy were not forgotten. The committee set apart £35 far the purpose of giving a treat to the aged poor, and to the wi- dows, and on Wednesday evening 510 old people gathered in the Publie Hall, and partook of a capital "meat tea." As many of the old people were too Infirm to walk, Mr. S. Yarwood and Mr. Peck kindly placed their conveyances at the disposal of these unfortenates. Ihe arranzements were in the hands of Messrs. F. Norman, H. Hughes, J. Whinyates, W. Pownall, jun., and J. A. Smith, and these gentlemen placed the feeding department under the control of Mr. R. (brat, confectioner, High-street, whose catering gave crmplote satisfaction. The following ladies assisted by presiding over the various tables:—Mrs W. Timmins. Ms F.. Imison, Mrs Findlay, Mrs. Towns. Mrs A. Riley, Mrs W. Pownall, jun., Mrs Sutton, Mrs Wright, Mrs W. Hughes, Mrs Ross, Mrs Mellor Mrs Cooke, and Mrs Frith ; Misses Dobson, Norman, dam tson,* Anderton Towns, Savage, Statham; A. Stattarn, Wright, Riley, Imison, P. Riley. A. Imison, and Owen. A large number of young men were a'se actively employed. The oldest person in the room was Mrs Wainwright. of Shaw-street. who had at- , tained the age of 96 years. The limit of age to ensure participation in the trust was 60 years. After tea, the public were admitted at a charge of 61. each to witness the entertainment, and a sum of upwards of £5 was thus rea- lised. Mr. Philip Speakman presided, and he was sup- ported by toe Revs W. Preston and J. D. Thomas; Messrs W.- Whittaker. J Pritchard, J R Frith, T Handley, H J Griee, S C Beck-R, W Handley, W Shaw, E Mar- sball, C Pownall, T Clegg, dm. A gay appearance had been imparted to the ball by a plentiful display of parti- coloured flags, and a profaelon of flowering and foliage plants from the greenhouses of the chairman adorned the platform. Behind. the p'atfortn was a coloured representa- tion of the Royal Arms flanked on each eide by tee Union Jack. Messrs S. Coventry and George Yarwood have car- ried out the decorations. The Chairman made a brief. speech in opening the pro- ceedings. After giving the old folks a hearty welcome, he said that there had been a great deal said about the Queen, but he did not think that se word too much bad been said, because a better ands nobler Qoeen never reigned ever any empire. (Loud anplause.) In Runcorn her Majesty had thousands of good citizens, and he thought it would be very becoming if they were to Send from that assembly a telegram to the Queen, congratulating her Majesty on.at- taining her Julaitee. (Applause.) Ha had just drafted the folloeing telegram :—"Queen Victoria,-500 aged poor of Runcorn enj tying Jubilee celebration, send heartiest con- gratulations to their Queen." (Applause.) Those in favour of that message going to their Queen say (t.oud cries of "Ah ) The Chairman then called for three cheers for the Queen,and a most enthusiastic response was made. In conclusion, he stated that 510 people had sat down totes that afternoon. The average age was 65 years, and the narnber' of years represented by these people was 33170. That wee a fackto think about. (Attplaus,..) The programme was glen proceedtd with. the band of the 2nd C.R.Y. opening by playing "god save the Queen,' after which the audience gave three cheere for her Majesty. During the evening Mr goiford'a Tonic-sal-fa Class 'sang several songs ie capital stifle. Mr, Thomas Riley gave a Loncashire reading entitled "The Russians at Constanti- nople " the audience much enjoying the ludicrous incidents described. A troupe of Local Charity Minstrels also gave an entertainment, it which the following WOO were.sung —" Out in the snow," J Leathwood ' • "I've lost my Mary Jane," J Birkett ; and My grandfather's moke," David ,Ballington. Mr .3 ,Wood played the cornet 'solo " Rule Bri,tania " with vkriatims. and he was rewarded for his skilful performance by loud applause. The troune sang several concered pieces. Mr Horace Handley was con- ductor and accompanist. At a later period the minstrels gave a laughable sketch. The ventriloquial perfermance et Professor Millar was a highly diverting feature of the entertainment. Mr Millar is a roost clever -entrilcquist, and the manner in which he made his figures talk, sine, and exchange jokes was a treat to witness, and the old people accented him an enthusiastic encore. The Gipsy chorus which recently perrirmed with such success at Bethesda Schoolroom. contributed greatly to the enjoyment of those present by their capital sidging and graceful dancing, Gran pbd on the stage in their gay attire they presented a pretty specticle which called forth many not 4 of admira- tion. At the conclusion the Rev. W. Preston proposed a vote of thanks to the chairman. In doing so he-remarked upon the good cendudt and proper behaviour that distinguished all concerned in.the previous day's proceedings, which be said were a credit to the town. There was one gentleman con- nected with the Juhilee demonstration to whom their thanks were justly due, and that was the cnairman, who had spared neither his time nor his money, but had given of both g-neeleusly, and with an ungrudging habd, and in an unos- tentatious manner. (Applause.) The Rev. J. D. Thomas seconded the motion. Mr. Speakman, as chairman of the Jubilee Committee, had worked very bard, and he had conducted their deliberations exceedingly well. The enteiteinment that evening was a St ine elm.° to his chairmanship of the Commissioners, and it was their sincere hope that he might live lone, and ti-at by and bye be would not be merely chairman of the Com- missione,s, but Mayor of the Borough of Runcorn. (Loud applause.)

THE Junit,El IN Ittasartn.-Sorne disturbances occurred in Dublin on Tuesday night, a crowd of boys pelting the police and smashing the windows of thelnew Orange Hall. A number of constables were struck with stones, and one of them badly but. The mob were at last dispersed in College Green after breaking one of the College windows. Over one hundred persons were injured at Cork on Tuesday night in the charges of the police. Sixty-one persons were treated at the infirmaries for cuts and bruisos, and three Or four had fractures of the skull. Black flags floated on Tuesday ham the Cork municipal offices, and various Nationalist mottoes were displayed, while many Nationalists wore crape on their left arms. Parties of Loyalists and Nationalists paraded the streets, the former singing the National Anthem and the latter "God save Ireland."

I after- w..rds tried several remedies which are advertised to cure rheumatism, but found them useless. and became completely discouraged, feeling that I should never be' able to walk gain. I owe my retura to health, and my present happiness all to St. Jacobs Oil, which I shall never be without again as long as I live." Price 28 6d, by post 24 94.

OUR FINANCIAL LETTER. .---- [FIIOISI OUR OWN CORRESPONDENT.] 23, Old Broad-street, B.C. It has been difficult to start business after the holiday& There has been a fair attendance in the " House," and tor a time the outlook seemed good. Prices opened fullrup to the average of last Monday, but as soon as it appeared that the market was more inclined to sell than to boy a reaction set in. Foreigners have been quiet until continental prices began to arrive, after which they relapeed. Egyptians, Turkish, Trebutes, Hungarians, Italians, and Spanish Fours, all inclining frantionally. Speculative South Americans were weak, but there was still a fair demand for investment bonds. Home railways do not show so much benefit as might have been expected from the holiday traffic. There can be no doubt it has been very large, and will make a good show in next week's returns The present" week's returns are, however, poor, having to compare with the Whit-week of last year. All stocks have been more or less affected by them. Acting on a market which had no backbone of its own, they gave prices another excuse for drooping. Mexi- can Railways have had a more tangible excuse for weakness, their traffic announcement being unsatisfactory. The bulls of this stock are wearying badly for the Ist of July, which is to give them the benefit of the reduced cus- toms tariff. They begin to need it greatly. Grand Trunks were exceptionally firm during the greater part of the day, though toward the close they also began to ease off. Among miscellaneous shares Hotchkiss took the lead with a fresh rise. strong buying in it becomes more and more ap- parent, and some shrewd dealers are said to be taking their I profits on stouts and beers. Continental Trams are for the moment quiet, but they are being well held.. Foreign Government Securities show considerable depres- sion, a dull and heavy tone beieg supported on the conti- nental Bourses.
